Over four quarters the company has relocated or decommissioned a meaningful share of its 60 kW and 120 kW units, redeploying them into depots leased by cab fleet operators and into a state transport undertaking's electric bus contract. Revenue per unit has roughly doubled on the assets that moved, according to a person who has seen the internal register. The public network is now, in effect, a marketing line.
The arithmetic of an idle connector

A 60 kW dual-gun charger lands at somewhere between 16 lakh and 22 lakh rupees installed, depending on transformer work and civil cost. Add a sanctioned-load augmentation, a dedicated feeder where the distribution utility insists on one, and a five-year maintenance contract, and the asset has to earn steadily for a long time before it becomes interesting.

Utilisation is the whole game. Below roughly 8 per cent of available hours, a public unit in a metro does not cover its demand charges, licence fee and network operations cost. Highway sites built ahead of demand routinely sit in low single digits outside long weekends. Depot units serving a fleet that must be charged between two shifts run several times that, on a schedule the operator controls.

Tariffs have improved without resolving the problem. Most states now notify a separate charging category, and several cap or defer the demand-charge component for an initial period. Where that concession has lapsed, operators report the fixed component alone exceeding the energy component in a weak month.

"We were paying industrial demand charges to sell four hours of electricity a day," said a network operations head at a charging company that has exited two highway corridors. "No amount of software fixes that. A bus depot fixes that."
Land, and the price of being visible

Early networks were built on the assumption that visibility drives usage, which pushed operators into malls, fuel forecourts and office basements on revenue-share or fixed-licence terms. The fixed licence fees, negotiated when charging looked like a land grab, have been the harder mistake to unwind; several run five to nine years with escalation clauses attached.

Revenue-share deals age better but carry their own difficulty. Mall operators increasingly want a share of the charging bill and the parking fee, and treat the bay as premium inventory during peak retail hours, which is precisely when a fast charger would otherwise be busy.

Enforcement is a small line item that behaves like a large one. Bays blocked by combustion vehicles, cut cables and vandalised payment terminals each cost a site visit, and operators who tried to run unmanned public sites at scale have quietly reintroduced attendants at their busiest fifth of locations.
The fleet book changes the credit question

Moving into depots converts a consumer business into a business-to-business one, with everything that implies. Setu now carries receivables from cab fleet operators and one state undertaking on terms of 45 to 75 days, against energy it has paid the distribution utility for within a fortnight. Working capital, not capital expenditure, has become the binding constraint.

Lenders have noticed. Two non-bank financiers active in charging assets said they now underwrite against a contracted offtake schedule rather than a location's traffic count, and price the difference at 250 to 400 basis points. A network without an anchor fleet is, in their language, an infrastructure asset carrying retail risk.

It changes the hardware too. Depot charging tolerates lower power per gun and higher connector counts; a bus depot wants overnight charging at 30 to 60 kW across many vehicles, not a 240 kW pull for one. Several operators are buying cheaper, denser equipment specified around a single fleet's duty cycle.

"Our best asset is a charger nobody sees," said Setu's chief operating officer, describing a depot installation outside Hosur. "It is behind a gate, it runs eleven hours a night, and it is the only site I do not worry about."
Supplier terms and the imported box

On the buy side, charger manufacturers have moved from advance payment to 30-day credit for operators with a record. But power electronics and connectors remain largely imported and dollar-priced. Operators who fixed customer tariffs in annual fleet contracts without hedging the equipment pipeline have absorbed the difference on replacement units.

Localisation is proceeding unevenly. Cabinets, cabling and installation are domestic. The rectifier module, the contactors and the payment-capable controller are not, and a phased manufacturing requirement attached to any future incentive would bite hardest at exactly that layer.
What the next round of capital will ask

Setu's next raise, which people familiar with the process expect to be a structured instrument rather than straight equity, will be judged on contracted energy throughput rather than connector count. That metric barely appeared in pitch decks two years ago.

The broader lesson is unglamorous. Public charging in India is turning out to be a utility business with a long ramp rather than a network-effects business, and the operators surviving the transition are those that stopped selling convenience and started selling scheduled kilowatt-hours to somebody obliged to buy them.

title: A second apprenticeship for the mechanics of Hosur
dek: In a cluster built on carburettors and clutch plates, garages are learning insulation ratings, torque values and the discipline of never working alone.

body.text: The first thing that changed at Sri Vinayaka Auto Electricals was the floor. The owner pulled up the oil-soaked matting, laid down a rubber sheet rated to a thousand volts, and painted a yellow rectangle around it. Nobody works inside that rectangle unless a second person is standing outside it. That rule, more than any tool he bought, is what he tells visitors the shop has learned.

His garage sits off the Krishnagiri road on the edge of Hosur, in a strip of two-bay workshops that have serviced the cluster's motorcycles, autorickshaws and light commercial vehicles for three decades. About a fifth of the vehicles that now come in have no engine. Almost every man who works on them learned the trade on carburettors.

Reskilling in the Indian automotive aftermarket is usually discussed as a number, some large figure of technicians who will need retraining by the end of the decade. On the ground it looks like this: a man of forty-four who can diagnose a fuel pump by sound being told that the most important skill in his new job is knowing when not to touch something.
What high voltage actually demands

The practical syllabus is short and unforgiving. Isolate the pack. Verify isolation with a meter rated for the job, then verify the meter. Wait for the capacitors to discharge. Use insulated tools, gloves tested to their class rating and stored unfolded, and a torque wrench, because a busbar bolt that is loose and a busbar bolt that is overtightened end the same way.

Little of this is intuitive to a technician trained on mechanical systems, where a wrong move produces a noise, a leak or a stripped thread. A high-voltage error produces nothing at all until it produces everything at once. Trainers say the hardest habit to install is the pause before the hands move.

"On a petrol vehicle the mistake tells you immediately," said an instructor who runs high-voltage modules for an automotive skills body in Tamil Nadu. "Here the vehicle stays silent and the man stays confident. That is the combination we are training out of them."
Who pays for the classroom

Formal certification exists. Sector skill council modules, dealer academies run by vehicle makers and a handful of private institutes offer courses of two to six weeks. The obstacle is not curriculum but wage loss. An independent workshop that sends two of its four technicians away for three weeks loses roughly half its throughput in a business that runs on daily cash.

The result is a two-track system. Authorised dealer workshops train through the manufacturer and are paid to do it. The independent aftermarket, which handles most out-of-warranty work and nearly all three-wheeler and small fleet repair, trains informally, in the evenings, or not at all. Fleet operators have begun filling the gap themselves.

One last-mile logistics firm running about 600 electric three-wheelers across Hosur, Krishnagiri and the Bengaluru periphery now operates a two-week internal course and pays a retention bonus at six months, having lost trained men to dealer workshops twice.

Pay has not moved much to match. A technician holding a high-voltage certificate earns perhaps fifteen to twenty per cent more at a dealer workshop, and frequently nothing extra at an independent one, where customers resist paying a diagnostic fee for a fault that takes a scanner and ten minutes to find.
The swapping station changes the work

Two kilometres away, a battery swapping station serves the same fleets. Its economics push work away from garages. A driver exchanges a discharged pack in under three minutes, and every cell-level problem becomes the swapping operator's, handled at a central facility with diagnostic equipment no roadside shop will ever buy.

That suits the drivers, who are paid per delivery and price each minute accordingly. It leaves the independent workshop with the rest of the vehicle: suspension, brakes, wiring, the controller, the charging port and the endless business of accident repair. Margins there are thinner than engine work ever was, because there is simply less to wear out.

"The engine was my annual income," said the owner of a two-bay shop on the same road that has been open since 1994. "Oil, filter, tuning, rings, every year something. Now they come for brakes and a broken indicator."
The spare parts problem nobody solved

Spares remain the sharpest constraint. Controllers, DC-DC converters and pack modules are rarely sold to independents, partly for liability reasons and partly because manufacturers prefer replacement at authorised points. Workshops therefore repair at board level, unofficially, using components sourced through grey channels in Chennai and Bengaluru.

Everyone involved knows what this is. It voids warranties, it leaves no trace, and when a repaired controller fails on a highway there is no recall path back to it. Insurers have started asking questions about repair provenance on total-loss claims, which may force the issue faster than any regulation.
Why the cluster keeps adapting

Hosur's advantage has always been proximity and volume. Assembly plants, component makers and a large two-wheeler manufacturing base sit within a short radius, and the workshops around them absorbed every previous shift: electronic ignition, fuel injection, then emission norms that made a diagnostic scanner compulsory equipment.

This transition differs in degree. It removes work rather than adding complexity to it, and it demands a safety discipline the trade has never needed. The owner of the shop with the yellow rectangle has decided the answer is to specialise in the parts of the vehicle that will still break, and to be the one garage on his road certified to open a pack. He has a single technician through the course and a second booked after the festival season, when the fleets are too busy to spare anybody.

title: The Ayush GMP deadline meets a base of micro manufacturers
dek: Revised good-manufacturing norms require testing capacity and technical staff that most of the country's licensed Ayurveda units have never had to carry.

body.text: The revised good manufacturing practice requirements for Ayurveda, Siddha and Unani manufacturing were notified with a transition period that looked generous on paper. Two years on, licensing officers in three states describe the same pattern in their files. The large units complied early. The mid-sized ones are part-way through capital work. The bottom of the register has not moved at all.

That bottom is most of the industry. The overwhelming share of Ayush manufacturing licences sit with units employing fewer than twenty people, many making a narrow list of classical formulations for local practitioners or working on job-work for larger brands. The revised obligations, which sort manufacturers by scale and product category, ask them for things a job-work unit has never carried: qualified technical staff on the rolls, in-house or contracted testing with documented results, and a pharmacovigilance reporting line.

The enforcement question is not whether the norms are right. It is what a state licensing authority does when a district's compliance rate sits under half and the alternative to enforcement is closing the units that supply the district's own dispensaries.
From premises to process

The substance of the revision is a shift in what an inspection looks at. Earlier inspections leaned on physical infrastructure: segregated areas, water supply, storage conditions. The revised framework retains all of that and adds documentation. Batch manufacturing records, raw material identity testing, finished product specifications, stability data supporting any shelf-life claim, and a designated technical person holding a recognised Ayush degree.

Testing is the expensive part. A basic laboratory able to run identity, moisture, ash value, heavy metals and microbial limit work costs a small unit more than its annual profit, and approved outside laboratories are unevenly distributed. In one state, licensing officers said practically all outsourced testing goes to laboratories in two cities, which sets an effective queue for every batch that leaves a small plant.

Raw material is the quieter half of the problem. A unit buying herb from a mandi trader is now expected to record species identity, supplier and test results for material that has historically moved on trust and a weighbridge slip. Several licensing officers said raw material documentation, rather than plant upgrades, is where renewals are actually failing.

"A unit can buy a building, it cannot buy a chemist in a district where none is available," said a state licensing officer who inspects Ayush manufacturing units. "We are refusing renewals for missing staff, not for missing walls."
The advertising file runs alongside

Separately, enforcement against exaggerated efficacy claims has hardened. After the rule requiring prior approval for Ayush advertisements was withdrawn, action has proceeded under the older statute on objectionable advertisements for drugs and remedies, and through the consumer protection regulator's route against misleading claims.

This has produced an odd asymmetry. A claim printed on a label is a drug licensing matter. The same claim in a television commercial is a consumer protection matter. The same claim made by an influencer on a short-video platform is difficult to attach to the manufacturer at all. Companies have adapted by pushing claims down the chain, away from the package.

Officials in two states said the binding constraint is cadre strength. Inspecting manufacturing units, drawing samples and monitoring advertising all draw on the same small drug control staff, sized years ago for a pharmaceutical caseload and never expanded to match the Ayush licence register.
Insurance and the district hospital wing

Policy has moved faster on the demand side. Ayush treatment is now covered by several health insurers for in-patient care at accredited facilities, and government schemes reimburse defined packages. Ayush wings have been sanctioned in district hospitals across most states under the national health mission.

The bottleneck there is accreditation and staffing rather than money. Practitioners in Kerala and Maharashtra said reimbursement requires documentation a small Panchakarma facility is not equipped to produce, and that empanelment surveys move slowly. Several clinics have concluded that the cash patient is simply less trouble.

"Insurance pays for the bed, not for the therapy," said an Ayurveda practitioner who runs a twenty-bed facility in central Kerala and has been empanelled for two years. "The oils, the therapist's hours, the fourteen days: that is the treatment, and the package rate does not see any of it."
What quiet consolidation would look like

The likely outcome is consolidation without an announcement. Larger manufacturers with compliant plants are already absorbing job-work that small units can no longer lawfully take, and loan licensing, where a brand manufactures at another company's licensed premises, is expanding for the same reason.

That is not automatically bad for quality, and regulators privately regard it as the point. It does change who owns the classical formulation trade, historically dispersed across thousands of small units linked to individual practitioners, many carrying formulations of local reputation and no brand at all.

Two state governments have floated cluster testing facilities, shared laboratories that small units can use at subsidised rates, on the model used in food processing. Where these exist, compliance rates are visibly higher. Where they were announced and never built, licensing officers report the same files gathering the same objections.
The deadline that will probably move

Industry associations have asked for a further extension and a partial one is widely expected. Officials involved in the drafting argue that each extension weakens the signal, and note that the last one produced almost no additional compliance until its final quarter.

The alternative under discussion is differentiated enforcement: strict application for units making patent and proprietary medicines that carry therapeutic claims, and a lighter, supervised pathway for classical formulations made to a pharmacopoeial text. It would be harder to administer. It would also be closer to how the industry actually works.

title: Where the rejected herbal consignments go
dek: A formulations exporter's returned lots trace a route into domestic supply that residue limits abroad were meant to close, and nobody is required to record it.

body.text: A container of ashwagandha root extract left Nhava Sheva in the spring and came back in the autumn. Between those dates it was tested at a laboratory in Rotterdam, found to carry a pesticide residue above the European limit for a herbal preparation, refused entry and shipped home at the consignor's cost. What happened to it after that is the part no register records.

Sahyadri Vanaushadhi Ltd, a Nashik-based formulations maker that contract-manufactures for four direct-to-consumer brands and exports under its own label, says the lot was destroyed. Two people who have worked in the trade's export segment said destruction is the exception. The economics point the other way. A rejected lot is worthless abroad and perfectly saleable at home, where the limit that failed it does not apply in the same form.

This is the uncomfortable centre of India's herbal export business. The country supplies a very large share of the world's traded ashwagandha, turmeric, senna and psyllium, and the same fields, the same collectors and often the same processing lines feed the export lot and the domestic one. The difference between them is a certificate.
Two standards, one supply chain

European buyers of herbal material work to maximum residue levels set for the finished preparation, along with limits on heavy metals, aflatoxins and microbial load, verified by accredited laboratories. Gulf regulators run a registration process with its own dossier requirements. Domestic requirements for Ayush products exist and have tightened, but the testing infrastructure that would make them binding on every batch does not yet reach the small manufacturer.

The result functions as a sorting mechanism rather than a quality floor. Material is tested, and the cleanest fraction is allocated to export orders. Everything else finds a buyer. Traders describe this openly, as a grading practice rather than a scandal, which is roughly how it operates.

"There is no bad lot, there is only a lot in the wrong market," said a commodity trader who has sourced medicinal plant material out of Neemuch and Unjha for two decades. "The buyer decides the specification and the specification decides the price."
A sourcing floor that keeps moving

Sahyadri's procurement head describes a market with no stable price. Ashwagandha root moved through a wide band over eighteen months as export demand collided with a poor season in the growing belts of Madhya Pradesh and Rajasthan. Shatavari and safed musli have been more volatile still. Cultivated material is more traceable and more expensive; wild-collected material is cheaper, less documented and, in a bad year, the only material available.

Companies with export commitments have responded by contracting acreage directly, supplying seed and buying back at a floor price. That works where a species is genuinely cultivable at scale. It does not work for the several dozen species still largely gathered from forests, where the chain runs through collectors, forest committees and mandi intermediaries, and the paperwork thins at every step.

Certification adds cost that only some buyers pay. Organic certification adds meaningfully to landed cost and requires three years of conversion on the land. Several exporters said European buyers want the certificate and then negotiate the premium away, while Gulf buyers care more about registration and shelf life.
Contract manufacturing hides the trail

The structural problem is that most Indian herbal brands do not manufacture. They buy finished goods from contract manufacturers, who buy extracts from processors, who buy raw material from traders, who buy from village-level aggregators. Each layer tests what its own buyer demands, and no more than that.

When a consignment fails abroad, the failure attaches to the exporter of record. The processor two layers down usually never learns which of its lots was implicated, and no mandatory mechanism exists that would tell it. The companies that have built genuine backward traceability did so because a single large buyer insisted on it.

"My customer audits me and I audit my extract supplier," said the quality head at a mid-sized contract manufacturer in Gujarat that supplies three export brands. "Below that, I am relying on a certificate of analysis I did not watch anybody produce."
Quick commerce reshapes the home market

Domestically the channel has shifted faster than the supply chain behind it. Quick-commerce platforms now account for a large and rising share of urban sales of churnas, oils and single-herb capsules, and they favour small pack sizes, wide assortment and rapid replenishment. That has pulled manufacturers into shorter production runs and far more frequent changeovers.

It has also changed the working capital shape. Platform terms look better than traditional distribution on paper, but listing fees, promotional funding and returns handling absorb the difference. A formulations maker that once shipped pallets to a stockist now ships cartons to a dark store, and carries the cost of that difference itself.
What would actually close the gap

Three remedies came up repeatedly in conversations across the trade. Mandatory residue testing at the processor rather than at the point of export, which puts the cost where material is aggregated. A working traceability requirement for wild-collected species, tied to the existing minor forest produce system. And a domestic specification that matches the export one, so a failed lot has nowhere cheaper to go.

None is imminent. The first two are administratively heavy, and the third would raise domestic prices in a market where the classical formulation trade competes hard on cost. Until then, the container that came back from Rotterdam stays a commercial problem for one exporter rather than a signal that travels back down the chain.

title: At Neemuch, the price of a root is still set by hand
dek: The busiest medicinal plant mandi grades ashwagandha by touch and smell each morning, while the laboratories that could settle the argument sit two days away.

body.text: By seven in the morning the arrivals shed at Neemuch is loud in a specific way. Not the clang of a grain mandi, but the low continuous sound of jute being cut open. Ashwagandha root, dried and cut, arrives in sacks of forty to sixty kilograms from Mandsaur, Ratlam, Jhalawar and further out. A commission agent walks the line, takes a piece from each opened sack, snaps it, smells the break and calls a price.

He is grading for colour, for the whiteness of the interior, for thickness and the absence of a woody core, and for moisture, which he judges by feel and confirms occasionally with a hand-held meter. The transaction takes under a minute a lot. The buyer standing behind him will ship the same material to an extraction plant that tests it against a dozen parameters the agent cannot see.

That gap, between the sensory grading that sets the farm-gate price and the analytical grading that sets the export price, is where most of the value in India's medicinal plant trade is captured. It is also where most of its disputes begin.
Two supplies meeting in one yard

The larger supply is cultivated. Ashwagandha, isabgol, coleus, senna and safed musli grown on contract or on speculation across western Madhya Pradesh and adjoining Rajasthan. Farmers here have grown medicinal crops long enough to read the market, and they hold stock when they can afford to hold it.

The smaller and older supply is gathered. Bark, roots, gums and fruit collected from forest fringes arrive through intermediaries, routed via forest committees or state minor forest produce federations where the species is regulated, and through informal channels where it is not. Collector households are paid something close to a daily wage for work that is seasonal, physically hard and priced at the bottom of a chain that ends in a capsule.

Rates for gathered material have improved where a federation fixes a procurement price and then actually lifts the stock. Where the federation announces a rate and does not buy, the announced rate is decorative and the trader's offer prevails.

"We are told the government rate, and then we sell at the rate the truck offers," said a collector from a forest-fringe village in the Chhindwara belt who brings gum and roots to an aggregator twice a season. "The truck comes to the village. The government does not."
Adulteration and how it gets caught

Adulteration in this trade is rarely dramatic. It is a matter of proportion. Stem mixed into root, an inferior species substituted where the dried material looks similar, sand or starch added for weight, old stock blended into new. Shatavari, safed musli and guggulu attract the most substitution, because the price gap between the true species and its lookalikes is wide enough to pay for the trouble.

Detection has improved without becoming routine. Thin-layer chromatography, high-performance liquid chromatography and, increasingly, DNA barcoding can settle a species question definitively. The constraint is turnaround and cost. A test that takes five days and a few thousand rupees cannot be applied to a lot that trades in an hour on a mandi floor.

The practical compromise is that testing happens after purchase, at the processor, and the commercial consequence travels backwards as a claim on the trader. Traders price that risk in. Farmers, furthest from any laboratory, absorb it as a lower opening bid on material they have no way to certify.
The laboratory two days away

A handful of accredited laboratories in Indore, Ahmedabad and Hyderabad do most of the analytical work for this trade. Samples travel by bus and courier. A pharmacopoeial laboratory and several state drug testing laboratories exist, but their capacity is committed to regulatory sampling rather than commercial grading, and the queue reflects it.

Attempts to move testing to the mandi have had mixed results. Portable near-infrared instruments can screen for moisture and gross adulteration in minutes, and two aggregators at Neemuch use them. Calibrating such an instrument for a botanical species, though, requires a reference library that has to be built and then maintained, and nobody in the yard is funded to maintain one.

"The machine is only as good as the samples you taught it with," said a laboratory manager in Indore whose facility tests medicinal plant material for three extraction companies. "For turmeric we have thousands of reference spectra. For a wild root from one district, we have eleven."
Cultivation as the slow correction

The direction of travel is toward cultivation, for the same reason it was in every other crop that industrialised. A buyer can specify, inspect and contract a field in a way it can never do with a forest. The national medicinal plants programme and several state horticulture missions subsidise planting material and post-harvest infrastructure for a defined species list, and the list keeps growing.

The species that resist cultivation are the ones that matter most, both to classical formulations and to conservation: slow-growing Himalayan and Western Ghats plants with narrow habitat requirements and long maturity. For those, the alternative to a functioning collection system is not a plantation. It is substitution, which is how a shortage quietly becomes an adulteration problem.

By eleven the shed is quieter. Lots are weighed, sacks restitched and trucks loaded for extraction plants in Gujarat and Andhra Pradesh, where the material will be tested properly for the first time. The price it fetched here was decided by a man breaking a root with his thumb.

title: Liquidity draft sends bank treasuries hunting for stickier deposits
dek: Higher run-off assumptions on digitally accessible deposits are pushing banks to reprice bulk money, reopen branches and reload their securities buffers.

body.text: The first thing a treasury head at a mid-sized private bank in Mumbai did after the Reserve Bank of India circulated its revised liquidity framework was open a list of the bank's thousand largest deposit relationships and colour each line. Green for balances that had not moved in two years. Amber for money that arrived on a corporate sweep instruction and left on the same instruction. Red for anything a customer could move at two in the morning from a phone, without speaking to anyone. By his own rough count, close to a third of the retail book came up red.

Some version of that exercise has been run at almost every scheduled commercial bank in the country this year. The proposal to attach an additional run-off factor to retail and small-business deposits that are accessible through internet or mobile banking reads like a technical adjustment to a ratio. It is not. It changes what a bank is willing to pay for different kinds of money, and therefore the shape of what it can afford to lend.

The liquidity coverage ratio asks a narrow question. If the next thirty days went badly, would the bank still hold enough high-quality liquid assets to meet what walks out of the door? Raise the assumed outflow on a large slice of deposits and the answer changes. Banks respond either by buying more government securities, which yield less than loans, or by chasing deposits the model treats as sticky. Most are doing both, and passing on the difference where they can.
Reading the run-off table

Compliance officers who have modelled the draft say the burden falls unevenly. A bank whose savings book rests on salary accounts in district towns, where the average balance is modest and the customer has banked at the same branch for a decade, comes out comparatively well. A bank that built its savings franchise quickly through digital onboarding, paying a higher rate on balances above a threshold, does not. The second model was, until quite recently, the one investors rewarded with a premium.

The modelling itself is unglamorous. Analytics teams have gone back through several years of transaction logs to sort accounts by channel of access, by whether the debit card was ever activated, by whether the customer also holds a loan, a locker or a recurring deposit with the same bank. Relationship depth has become a liquidity variable rather than a marketing one. One large lender now scores every retail account on an internal stickiness index that feeds straight into branch incentives.

"We are not being asked to hold more liquidity because we became riskier," said a treasury head at a mid-sized private bank who has submitted comments on the draft through an industry association. "We are being asked to hold more because our depositors now carry the branch around in their pocket."
The scramble for stickier money

The visible consequence is in deposit pricing. Special tenor buckets of 400 and 444 days, senior citizen premiums, and callable against non-callable differentials on bulk deposits have all been reworked since the draft appeared. Certificates of deposit, which had become a convenient way to plug a funding gap at quarter end, are being issued more sparingly by banks that would rather not show a large block of wholesale money attracting a high run-off assumption in the same statement.

Branch expansion has quietly returned to capital plans. Several lenders that had slowed physical rollout in favour of digital acquisition are opening again in tier-three and tier-four locations, on the reasoning that a deposit gathered across a counter behaves differently from one gathered through an application on a phone. The cost of acquisition per account is higher that way. Under the new arithmetic, so is the regulatory value of the resulting balance.
Where the cost eventually lands

Internal funds transfer pricing is the mechanism through which all of this reaches borrowers. Every bank runs a system that charges its lending desks for the money they use and credits its deposit-gathering desks for the money they raise. Treasuries have spent the last two quarters rewriting those curves, loading the liquidity cost on to short-tenor working capital and on to segments that consume liquidity without contributing stable balances in return.

Corporate borrowers have started to notice, mostly in the form of harder conversations about cash management mandates. A bank that once treated a current account as a relationship courtesy now wants the salary accounts, the vendor payments and the collection float alongside the credit line, because those balances score better in the model. Mid-market companies with a single banking relationship have the least room to argue.

"Nothing in the term sheet says liquidity coverage ratio," said a compliance officer at a public sector bank who reviews funds transfer pricing changes. "It shows up as ten or fifteen basis points on a renewal, and the borrower is simply told that the cost of funds has moved."
Smaller banks want a longer runway

Small finance banks and the larger urban cooperative banks have asked for a phased transition. Their submissions argue that their deposit franchises are younger, more concentrated and considerably more expensive to replace, and that they already hold their liquid buffers almost entirely in government securities. An increase in the requirement therefore translates fairly directly into a lower loan-to-deposit ratio and slower credit growth in precisely the segments that policy elsewhere is trying to fund.

The counterargument, made by officials whenever similar concerns have been raised, is that liquidity rules exist for the evening a rumour spreads on a messaging application and a queue forms before the branch opens. Supervisory post-mortems of two bank failures abroad in recent years described the mechanism in almost exactly those terms, and were circulated widely among Indian risk committees afterwards.

A final circular and an effective date are still awaited, and industry bodies expect some softening at the margins. Most treasuries have stopped waiting. Funding plans for the year have been built on the assumption that the draft survives broadly intact, on the reasoning that the cost of being wrong in the other direction, and having to buy liquidity in a hurry, is far higher than the cost of carrying a few hundred crore rupees of extra government paper.

title: A microfinance lender's cost of funds catches up with its book
dek: Kaveri Credit is repricing liabilities, tightening underwriting and converting branches to gold loans as securitisation investors demand more cover.

body.text: Ninety-four basis points is not a dramatic number. It is what Kaveri Credit Ltd, a Chennai-headquartered lender to joint-liability groups of women across four states, has added to its blended cost of funds over five quarters. On a book that is almost entirely small-ticket and unsecured, it is the difference between a company that can price a fresh microfinance loan where its competitors price theirs and one that cannot. Disbursements in the last completed quarter were the lowest the company has reported in three years.

The squeeze has three sources and only one of them is about Kaveri. Bank term loans, which fund a little more than half its liabilities, have repriced upward as lenders reassess their exposure to unsecured retail credit. Securitisation investors want thicker credit enhancement than they did eighteen months ago. And the underlying asset, small loans to rural households with no collateral behind them, has begun to behave worse than sector models assumed it would.

A rating agency moved the outlook on the company's long-term instruments to negative last quarter, citing slippage in asset quality and a thinner on-balance-sheet liquidity buffer. Executives have not disputed the reasoning. What they dispute, in private, is the idea that the stress is uniform across geographies, which is also the argument they are making to every lender who asks.
A funding mix under repair

The liability side is being rebuilt in real time. Direct assignment deals, in which a bank buys a pool of loans outright, have held up better than pass-through certificates, partly because the buyers are the same banks that already lend to the company and know the portfolio. Spreads on both have widened. A co-lending arrangement with a public sector bank, signed with some fanfare last year, is still stuck at the systems integration stage, which means it contributes nothing to this year's plan.

An attempt to place non-convertible debentures with domestic mutual funds did not clear the funds' internal credit committees at the coupon the company wanted to pay. External commercial borrowing was examined and set aside once the hedging cost was added. The treasury's answer, for now, is to hold more idle cash than it would like, which protects the rating narrative and costs real money every month it sits there.

"Pools that cleared at a certain spread eighteen months ago now need more cash collateral and a shorter tenor," said a structuring banker who has arranged three microfinance securitisation transactions this year. "The investor is not saying no. The investor is saying, price it as though it can go wrong."
The problem that started in Karnataka

The asset-side stress traces back to a handful of districts. A state ordinance aimed at coercive recovery practices by unregistered moneylenders was read in many villages as something broader, and repayment discipline in the affected blocks fell within weeks. Registered lenders operating under the central bank's directions found themselves lumped in with the operators the ordinance was written for. Collection efficiency in those branches has recovered only partly.

The second-order damage is to staffing. Field officers who were shouted at in a centre meeting, or told by a local functionary to stop visiting, do not stay in the job long. Branches in the affected districts have been running below sanctioned strength for two quarters, and rebuilding a centre once it has stopped meeting takes far longer than letting one lapse. The company has moved supervisors from Tamil Nadu to hold the line, at a cost.
Guardrails that shrink the pool

Underwriting has tightened everywhere at once. The regulator's directions replaced the older cap on the number of lenders per borrower with a limit on total household debt servicing as a share of monthly household income. Industry self-regulation then added a ceiling on the number of microfinance lenders to a single borrower and on aggregate exposure. Each rule is defensible on its own. Together they have shrunk the pool of borrowers a branch can lend to without shrinking the branch.

That arithmetic is unforgiving. The rent, the safe, the officer's salary and the branch manager's salary are all fixed. If the eligible borrower universe within a fifteen-kilometre radius falls by a fifth, operating cost per rupee lent rises immediately, and the only levers left are ticket size, which the guardrails also constrain, or a different product.
Gold, and other ballast

The different product is gold. Kaveri has begun converting a portion of its branch network to offer loans against jewellery alongside the group book, hiring appraisers, installing safes and building the auction discipline that the business needs to survive a fall in gold prices. Yields are lower than on microfinance. So is the capital requirement, and so, importantly, is the cost of the funding that lenders are willing to extend against a secured book.

"A gold loan does not need a bureau report and it does not need a centre meeting," said a senior executive at the company, who asked not to be identified because the audited numbers are not yet public. "It needs a weighing scale, a safe, and somebody who can tell twenty-two carat from eighteen."
What the sector watches next

Several smaller NBFC-MFIs have begun sounding out buyers for their portfolios, and at least two mid-sized players are understood to be in conversations about a merger that would give the combined entity the scale to argue for a small finance bank licence. Investors who funded the sector's last growth phase at high multiples are unlikely to be made whole in those transactions, which is the main obstacle to them closing.

The larger question, and the one lenders keep asking in credit committee meetings, is whether this is a cyclical correction in a business that has recovered from worse, or a permanent repricing of a model built on the assumption that unsecured group lending in rural India carries very little loss. Nobody underwriting a term loan this year is willing to assume the first answer without a secured book alongside it.

title: Seven in the morning, eighteen passbooks and one rejection to explain
dek: A field officer's centre meeting in rural Bihar shows how conduct rules and indebtedness caps have rewritten microfinance work on the ground.

body.text: The mat goes down a little after seven, on the concrete apron outside a house in a village in Muzaffarpur district, where the litchi orchards begin about two hundred metres behind the hand pump. Eighteen women arrive over the next twenty minutes, most carrying a passbook, one carrying a grandchild. The centre leader counts heads before the field officer does. By twenty past, instalments are being counted out in hundred-rupee notes and stacked under a stone so the wind does not take them.

The officer is twenty-six, from Sitamarhi, and has held the job for three years, which in this business makes him experienced. He carries a phone with the branch application on it, a spare power bank, a paper register that nobody trusts the application enough to abandon, and a laminated identity card the rules now require him to display where borrowers can read it. The card is newer than the register.

Almost everything about this half-hour is more documented than it used to be. Attendance is marked in the app. The stated purpose of each loan is recorded. Consent for the credit bureau enquiry is captured before the enquiry, not after it. The grievance redressal number is painted on the branch wall in Hindi and English and read aloud at the start of the meeting, which takes about forty seconds and to which nobody appears to listen.
The paperwork before the money

The real work happens before a rupee is disbursed. The lender must assess household income and ensure that total debt servicing across all lenders stays within the prescribed share of it. In a village where income arrives as a litchi crop, a paddy crop, money sent from a brother in Punjab, and the takings of a small shop that keeps no accounts, this is a structured conversation rather than a document check. Two officers and a supervisor sign off on the estimate.

Then the bureau enquiry runs. Between the regulator's household indebtedness limit and the industry's own ceiling on the number of microfinance lenders to a single borrower, a woman who has repaid on time for years can still be declined because her son took a two-wheeler loan and her husband has a consumer durable instalment running. There is an appeal of sorts, which involves the branch manager and a fresh income assessment, and which mostly does not change the answer.

"Earlier my job was to explain the interest rate. Now it is to explain the rejection," said a branch manager who supervises eleven field officers in the district. "She has repaid us for six years and the screen says no. There is no way to make that sound to her like a system that is working."
When the group does not close

Joint liability is no longer a contractual obligation in the way it once was, but the centre still behaves as though it is. When one member's payment is short, the others discuss it before the officer intervenes, and the money is usually found, sometimes from a relative and sometimes from a lender the group would prefer not to mention. The officer records the collection as received from the borrower, because that is what the receipt says.

Repayment follows the agricultural calendar closely. Collections are strong through the litchi harvest in May and June, sag during paddy transplanting when cash goes to labour and diesel, and recover after the crop is sold. Wedding season is the reliable disruption. Experienced officers set instalment dates against that calendar and mostly leave them alone, because a centre that has met on the same weekday for four years is an asset the branch cannot easily rebuild.
Collections after the code

The conduct rules have changed the choreography of recovery. Visits outside permitted hours are prohibited. Contacting relatives and neighbours about a borrower's dues is prohibited. Third-party agencies are engaged only for accounts well past ninety days, their staff carry identity cards issued in the lender's name, and tele-calling scripts are recorded and sampled by an internal audit team that calls a small share of borrowers back to check what was said to them.

What has not changed is the social mechanics underneath. A former recovery agent in the same block now does field verification for a gold-loan branch two towns away and describes the old work without much nostalgia. Sitting on a charpai outside a house at four in the afternoon, saying nothing to anybody, breaks no rule at all. It is also, everyone involved understands, the point.

"They come at the right time now, and they say the right things," said a centre leader who has held the group together for six years and has taken four loans herself. "But if I do not pay, everybody in this lane knows by evening. That was never written in any rule."
What the job actually pays

The officer handles roughly 480 borrowers across 22 centres on a six-day week. His pay is a fixed salary with an incentive tied to collection efficiency and to new borrowers who clear the eligibility filter, which is the part that has become harder. There is a fuel allowance that does not cover the fuel. Attrition among field staff at this level runs high enough across the sector that his branch has budgeted for replacing two of its six officers this year.

He has written the state bank clerical examination twice and intends to write it again in the winter. In the meantime the cash is counted, tallied against the app, sealed and deposited at the branch before eleven. The mat is rolled up and put back inside the house. His next centre meets at a quarter past eight, four kilometres away, and the phone syncs the morning's entries only when he reaches the highway and the network returns.

title: India's biosimilar pathway moves the proof from the ward to the lab
dek: A waiver of comparative efficacy trials shifts the burden on to analytical comparability, and the industry is asking regulators for predictability.

body.text: The revised guidance on similar biologics does something regulators do not often do. It takes a study away. Where a manufacturer can demonstrate that its molecule matches the reference product across a full analytical comparability package and a pharmacokinetic study in humans, the comparative efficacy trial in patients, long the slowest and most expensive stage of an Indian biosimilar programme, may be waived on justification.

For the companies, that is potentially a year and a half of development time and a large share of the budget. For the clinical research ecosystem that grew up around those trials, principal investigators, site coordinators, contract research organisations working the oncology and rheumatology wards, it is a business line contracting. For everyone else it is an argument about where confidence comes from: a few hundred patients, or a mass spectrometer.

The direction is not peculiar to India. European and British regulators have moved along similar lines, and the World Health Organization revised its own guidance in the same direction. What is being tested here is whether Indian sponsors can carry the analytical burden that replaces the trial, and whether Indian assessors have the bandwidth to interrogate it.
Fewer patients, more instruments

The package that replaces the trial is not cheap. It requires charge variant profiling, peptide mapping, detailed glycan analysis, higher-order structure work, potency measured by more than one orthogonal cell-based assay, forced degradation studies, and equivalence ranges built statistically from multiple lots of the reference product sampled across its shelf life. Sourcing those reference lots, legitimately and with documented cold chain, is itself a project that regulatory consultants say sponsors routinely underestimate.

That capability sits in a small number of laboratories. Larger firms have built it in house over a decade. Smaller sponsors outsource, and the queue at the better characterisation labs has lengthened noticeably since the draft circulated. The cost is front-loaded rather than lower, and it is repeatable across programmes, which favours companies with several molecules in development over those with one.

"The burden of proof has moved from the ward to the analytical laboratory," said a regulatory consultant who has prepared biosimilar dossiers for India and three emerging markets. "That is manageable if the comparability protocol is written before the first engineering batch. It is very expensive if it is written afterwards."
Sites, committees and the queue

None of this removes the regulatory machinery around trials that still run. Ethics committees must be registered and periodically re-registered with the central licensing authority, applications carry statutory timelines with deemed approval at the end of them, and site inspections continue. Investigators describe a familiar list of recurring findings: gaps in informed consent documentation, audio-visual recording requirements for vulnerable participants, source data that does not reconcile with the case report form, and temperature logs for investigational product that stop for a weekend.

What has shifted is the mix of work. Clinicians at two large teaching hospitals say the biosimilar trials that once filled their research calendars are being replaced by global multi-centre studies of novel molecules, which pay better and demand more, and by first-in-human work that a handful of units are equipped to do. The healthy-volunteer pharmacokinetic studies that biosimilar programmes still require are concentrating in a smaller number of specialised clinical pharmacology units.

Regulatory consultants add a practical caution. A waiver is granted on justification, not by right, and the assessor who reads the dossier is entitled to conclude that a residual uncertainty, an unexplained difference in a glycan profile or an immunogenicity signal in the pharmacokinetic study, warrants patients after all. Sponsors that treat the waiver as the default and design the programme around it risk discovering the requirement eighteen months late, when the reference product lots they characterised are close to expiry.
Regulated markets set the harder bar

Companies that intend to file in the European Union or the United States will assemble the fuller package regardless of what the Indian pathway permits, which produces a two-track development model inside the same organisation. The domestic-only filers will not, and that gap is what worries regulatory affairs heads asked about the change. Procurement agencies in Africa and Latin America read Indian approvals as a signal, and a perception that the domestic standard is the lighter one is difficult to argue against in a tender document.

The obligations that follow approval therefore matter more, not less. Risk management plans, product-specific pharmacovigilance, batch-level traceability and distinguishable naming are the mechanisms by which a waiver granted on analytical grounds is checked against what happens in patients. Industry submissions have asked for those requirements to be spelled out with the same specificity as the comparability expectations.
The request is predictability

The rest of the industry's comments are procedural rather than scientific. Sponsors want scientific advice meetings before submission, with written minutes that can be relied upon later. They want published assessment summaries so that a precedent set for one molecule is visible to the next applicant. They want a clear position on interchangeability and on what a pharmacist may substitute, and they want the central authority and state licensing authorities to read manufacturing requirements the same way.

"We can plan around a demanding standard," said the head of regulatory affairs at a Hyderabad-based biologics manufacturer. "We cannot plan around an unpredictable one, and the difference between those two is a scientific advice meeting that produces a written record."

The comment period has closed and subject expert committee meetings are working through the responses. The real test arrives with the first two or three dossiers that seek the waiver, and with whether the assessors grant it, refuse it, or ask for the trial anyway. Development plans across a dozen companies are, for the moment, being written both ways.

title: An empty bioreactor hall and the case for building it anyway
dek: Sahyadri Biologics is weighing a capacity bet on contract manufacturing enquiries that are rising far faster than signed tech transfer agreements.

body.text: The floor of the second bioreactor hall at Sahyadri Biologics' site in Ranjangaon, on the road out of Pune towards Ahmednagar, is still bare epoxy. The utilities are already in: the purified water loop, clean steam, and the ducting for a corridor that will separate the upstream suite from the fill line. What is missing is roughly forty crore rupees of single-use equipment, and a decision the company has now said it will take by the end of the quarter twice.

Sahyadri is fifteen years old, makes a small portfolio of biosimilars, and has spent the last four years building a contract development and manufacturing business alongside them. It is running the arithmetic every mid-sized Indian biologics company is running at the moment. Its own pipeline does not justify the capacity on its own. The contract pipeline might, if the enquiries convert into signed tech transfers, and that is the part nobody will underwrite.

Enquiry volume is not the constraint. Executives at three Indian contract manufacturers describe the same shape: a sharp rise in first conversations with American and European biotechs looking to hold manufacturing in more than one geography, and a far slower rise in agreements that actually start.
Enquiries are not orders

The gap between the two is filled with audits. A client evaluating an Indian site asks for inspection history, deviation and out-of-specification trends over two years, change control records, the training matrix for contractors, and evidence that the quality unit can stop a batch without asking the plant head. Then comes a tech transfer that takes eighteen to twenty-four months, during which the manufacturer carries the cost of a suite that is producing engineering runs rather than revenue.

Pricing is a thinner advantage than the pitch decks suggest. In biologics, the bioreactors, the single-use bags and tubing sets, the resins and much of the media are imported, so the input cost gap against a European site is modest. What India actually sells is engineering and validation talent at a fraction of Western cost, and the ability to staff three shifts of qualified operators without a recruitment crisis. That is a real advantage and a narrower one than the headlines imply.

"Everybody wants to be told that we are the alternative," said a business development head at a Pune-based biologics manufacturer. "Then they ask for the last three inspection reports and the deviation trend, and within an hour the conversation has become an audit rather than a sale."
The week the inspectors came

An inspection by a European regulator earlier this year concentrated on the areas that have become standard: environmental monitoring trends in the aseptic core rather than individual excursions, the handling and investigation of out-of-specification results, and the audit trail review practices for chromatography and bioreactor control software. Observations were closed with a corrective action plan, but the exercise consumed a quarter of the quality unit's year.

The internal consequences outlast the visit. Quality headcount has risen, a data integrity remediation programme now runs across both sites, and the company has decided to standardise on a single electronic batch record system rather than maintaining two. None of that shows up as capacity. All of it is a precondition for the contracts the capacity is being built for, and it is the line item finance departments find hardest to defend.

"An observation is not the expensive part," said a quality head at an Indian biologics site who has been through four regulatory inspections. "The expensive part is that every client audit for the next two years opens with that observation, and you spend the first morning of each one explaining it again."
Where the molecules actually sell

On the biosimilar side, the domestic market is a difficult place to fund a capital programme. Prices for the first wave of monoclonal antibodies have fallen sharply since they came off patent here, with several manufacturers competing on a molecule that a mid-sized hospital buys on tender. Margin now comes from exports, through partners who hold the registration in Latin America and South-East Asia, and those registrations take years to obtain.

Tender-driven markets bring their own problem, which is lumpiness. A large order fills a plant for two quarters and then does not repeat, and a facility built for that rhythm sits idle in between. That is precisely the case for the contract business: not because service margins are better, because they are not, but because they arrive in a steadier pattern and are paid for in advance of delivery.

Sahyadri's own answer is to sell capacity in slots rather than in campaigns, offering process development and a small number of good manufacturing practice batches to companies that need clinical supply rather than commercial volume. Margins on that work are thin and the scheduling is awkward, but it fills a suite between larger programmes and it introduces the site to sponsors who may need commercial capacity in three years, which is roughly the horizon the empty hall is being built against.
The winter one floor up

The picture is harsher for the platform companies, the cell therapy, mRNA and synthetic biology startups that raised money three and four years ago. Follow-on rounds have been slow. Public agency grants keep laboratories running but do not pay for a compliant manufacturing suite, and several founders have quietly turned their platforms into service offerings to generate cash. Talent has moved with the money, from startups towards established manufacturers with order books.

Sahyadri intends to fund the hall from internal accruals plus a structured debt facility, having considered and shelved a minority stake sale at the valuation it was offered. Two tech transfers are scheduled to begin within the year. If both slip a quarter, the equipment arrives into an empty building and the interest cost lands in a year with no revenue to set it against. That risk, one executive said, is the entire decision.

title: Hour fifty-one of a seventy-two hour run in Genome Valley
dek: Inside a shared bioprocess floor near Hyderabad, where the scale-up gap, the cold chain and a wage war for technicians all meet at night.

body.text: At twenty to two in the morning the loudest thing on the pilot floor is the chiller. A technician in a blue gown reads a dissolved oxygen trace off a screen, writes the value into a paper log because the electronic system here is validated only for the downstream suite, and lifts the agitation setpoint by fifty revolutions. The 200-litre fed-batch run is at hour fifty-one of about seventy-two. Nobody goes home in the middle of a run.

The floor belongs to a bioincubator off the Shameerpet road in Genome Valley, north of Hyderabad, which rents bioprocess capacity by the hour to companies too large for a university bench and far too small for a plant. Utilities, water for injection, clean steam, gowning and waste handling are shared. Twelve companies use the suites, and the calendar is booked several weeks ahead, which means a failed run costs a slot as well as a batch.

This is the step that Indian biotechnology is thinnest at. A laboratory result at two litres is not a process. A commercial facility will not take a process that has never run above ten. The equipment that bridges the two is expensive, idle much of the time, and almost impossible for an early-stage company to justify owning, which is the entire argument for a shared floor.
Twelve hours, then twelve more

The people who run it are not the people the sector talks about. Most technicians on the floor hold an ITI certificate or a diploma, a few have a bachelor's degree in microbiology or biotechnology, and all of them were trained on the job. The skills that matter are aseptic technique, a steady hand with a sampling port, and the discipline to write down what was done at the moment it was done rather than at the end of a shift. Runs are twelve hours, on a rotating roster.

Wages are the incubator's persistent problem. A technician with two documented campaigns behind them is worth thirty to forty per cent more to a contract manufacturer in Vizag or Bengaluru than the incubator pays, and the manufacturers know exactly who to call. The building has become a training academy for an industry that did not commission it, and its supervisors have stopped being surprised when a resignation arrives three weeks after a successful scale-up.

"I can teach somebody the sequence in three weeks," said a floor supervisor who has been running fermentations for eleven years. "Teaching them to record what they actually did, at the moment they did it, and not what the protocol says should have happened, takes about a year."
The cold chain nobody photographs

One floor down is the part of the building that never features in a brochure. Rows of minus eighty freezers holding cell banks, liquid nitrogen dewars in vapour phase for master stocks, all of it on generator backup with an automatic changeover that is tested at six every Wednesday morning because that is when the fewest runs are at a critical stage. Excursion alarms go to three phones, one of which belongs to a person who lives eleven minutes away by road.

For the two clients working on cell therapy the logistics are tighter still. A patient's cells arrive in a validated dry shipper with a charge that must be documented, and the finished product goes back on a clock that is measured in days and counted from a hospital bed. A customs hold, a rescheduled flight or a dewar that arrives warmer than its specification does not produce a delayed shipment. It produces a deviation, a discarded batch and a conversation with a treating physician.
Hiring for the other half

The bioinformatics vacancies are harder to fill than the floor vacancies. Sequencing volumes have risen across the incubator's tenants and every one of them wants someone who can maintain an analysis pipeline, version it, and defend the output to a regulator. Those candidates are also wanted by information technology services firms and by pharmaceutical analytics units, both of which pay more and neither of which requires anyone to be in a building at two in the morning.

"The graduates can run the tool," said a manager who handles hiring for the incubator and its tenants. "Very few of them have been taught to qualify the tool, document the version, and explain to an auditor why the result can be relied on. That is the gap, and it is not a coding gap."

An apprenticeship programme run with a state skills mission has begun placing diploma holders into six-month stints on the floor, with a bioprocess operations curriculum written by supervisors rather than by a university department. Placement rates have been good, which the incubator regards as evidence that the shortage was never really about the supply of graduates.
The step this building cannot take

What the incubator cannot supply is the next scale. A process proven at 200 litres still has to demonstrate itself at two thousand before a commercial partner will take it seriously, and that suite costs more than any tenant in the building can raise on current terms. Companies that get that far leave, either to a contract manufacturer's slot or to their own site, and the incubator loses its most advanced tenants precisely when they become interesting.

A proposal for a 500-litre suite in the adjoining block has been with funding agencies for a while. In the meantime the shift changes at six. The night technician hands over the log, the trace on the screen is still climbing, and a sample goes across to quality control in an insulated box small enough to carry in one hand.

title: As import parity climbs, the nutrient subsidy math stops adding up
dek: Subsidy rates were fixed against a phosphate market that has since moved, leaving importers to carry the gap through the sowing season.

body.text: The rate table that decides what a farmer in Vidarbha pays for a bag of di-ammonium phosphate was fixed months ago, in a quarter when imported phosphoric acid still looked like it was heading down. It has not headed down. Between the contract settled for the quarter and the landed cost of a cargo discharged at Kandla last week sits a gap that somebody has to carry, and under the nutrient-based subsidy regime that somebody is almost always the importer.

The design is simple enough on paper. The Centre fixes a per-tonne subsidy for each of nitrogen, phosphorus, potash and sulphur ahead of kharif and rabi, and leaves the maximum retail price of phosphatic and complex fertilisers formally decontrolled. In practice the price of DAP is not decontrolled at all. It sits where the government would like it to sit, and the industry keeps it there.

That worked while raw material prices were soft. It works less well now. Three fertiliser marketing executives, none of whom would allow themselves or their companies to be identified, described the same sequence over the past two seasons: bookings deferred, letters of credit opened later in the month, and a quiet shift of the sales pitch away from straight DAP towards complexes where the pricing has genuine room in it.
Where the arithmetic comes apart

Work through a notional tonne. Cost and freight for DAP, the rupee, ocean freight from the Gulf or North Africa, port handling, bagging, primary freight to a district warehouse and the dealer margin all have to fit inside the retail price plus the notified subsidy. When the first of those numbers moves by fifty dollars and the last two are fixed by convention, the contribution per tonne turns negative and stays negative for as long as the shipment takes to sell.

The response is a mix shift. Complexes such as 10:26:26 and 20:20:0:13 carry less phosphorus per bag, draw subsidy on the same nutrient logic and can be priced with a little more latitude. Sales teams push them. Agriculture extension officers, who spend the season explaining that a complex is not an equivalent of DAP on every soil and every crop, push back.

"We do not stop importing because the margin is negative," said the head of fertiliser marketing at a west coast importer, who was not authorised to discuss pricing. "We stop importing because the bank stops funding a negative margin."
The urea line on the import bill

Urea sits in a different regime and carries a different problem. Its retail price is statutory, its subsidy is calculated close to cost, and its consumption keeps climbing because it remains the cheapest nutrient a farmer can buy. Successive governments have tried to close the import gap by building. The revived plants at Ramagundam, Gorakhpur, Barauni and Sindri were meant to take domestic capacity to a point where imports became a residual rather than a habit.

They have narrowed the gap without closing it. Gas linkage, plant availability and the sheer growth in application all bite. The export side of the world market has thinned at the same time: Chinese shipments now move in and out according to Beijing's own reading of domestic availability, and a tender that once drew a dozen offers can draw five.

Officials in the Department of Fertilisers have talked for years about moving urea into the nutrient-based regime, which would let its price rise and slow the skew away from phosphorus and potash. No government has been willing to do it in a year with an election in it, and there is nearly always a year with an election in it.
The potash India does not mine

Potash is the starkest line on the bill. India imports effectively all of it, from Canada, Russia, Belarus, Israel and Jordan, on annual contracts negotiated by a small group of buyers. When those talks run late, the season opens without a settled price, and a subsidy notified in advance may or may not match what the cargo eventually costs when it berths.

The mines ministry's answer has been to put glauconite and potash-bearing blocks into auction in Rajasthan and Uttar Pradesh, alongside the wider critical mineral rounds covering graphite, vanadium and rare earth ground in the eastern states. Bids have come in. Blocks have been awarded. Almost none of it is producing, because a block in India is a licence to begin a process of forest clearance, land acquisition, drilling and pilot metallurgy that runs for years before a tonne moves.

"An auction is not a mine, and a mine is not a beneficiation plant," said a consulting geologist who has evaluated three of the auctioned blocks for prospective bidders. "We keep announcing the first of those three and costing the season as though we already had the third."
What the counter looks like in September

At the district level none of this is abstract. Sales run through point-of-sale machines that authenticate the buyer and release the subsidy to the manufacturer only when the bag actually crosses the counter, which means a retailer's working capital sits inside stock the company has already shipped and not yet been paid for. When supply looks uncertain, retailers stop lifting full rakes, and the shortage compounds itself.

A joint director in a western state's agriculture department described spending most of last month on the telephone to two companies and one railway divisional office, chasing rakes that had been allotted, loaded and then diverted to a neighbouring state where the sowing window had opened earlier. His department's own buffer, he said, is now measured in days rather than weeks.

There is a second-order effect that the enforcement wing worries about more. Subsidised urea is a cheap source of nitrogen for plywood resins, cattle feed and a handful of other industrial uses, and every season of tight availability at the counter is also a season of leakage away from it. Inspections rise in step with scarcity. Prosecutions rarely follow them.

None of this is an argument for scrapping the nutrient-based subsidy, which did what it was designed to do when it replaced a product-wise regime that rewarded whoever produced the most tonnage. It is an argument for setting the rates against something that moves. As things stand the rate is fixed twice a year against a market that reprices weekly, and the difference is financed, quietly and expensively, on the balance sheets of the people who import.

title: Vraj Speciality builds a new block into the worst pricing in a decade
dek: The Gujarat intermediates maker is commissioning capacity while realisations fall, betting that customer qualifications outlast Chinese oversupply.

body.text: The board of Vraj Speciality Chemicals cleared the second phase of its Dahej site in the same week the sales desk cut list prices on two of its largest agrochemical intermediates for the third time in a year. The two decisions are not in tension, the company's management argues. They are the same decision, taken at different points on the same curve.

Vraj is an unlisted Gujarat maker with an older plant at Ankleshwar and a newer one at Dahej, selling intermediates into crop protection and, increasingly, into pharmaceutical customers looking for a second source outside China. Its dispatched volumes have grown for eight straight quarters. Its revenue has not. That combination is the defining condition of Indian speciality chemicals at the moment, and it is not obvious how long a mid-sized private company can hold it.

The deflation is not a demand story. Indian formulators are buying, and so are Chinese ones. The pressure comes from the other side of the equation. Capacity added in Jiangsu, Shandong and Hubei during the last upcycle came on stream into a slower world, and producers with written-down assets and cheaper power have been willing to sell close to cash cost to keep their reactors turning over.
Volumes up, realisations down

Contracts in this business reprice quarterly, sometimes monthly, against a published or negotiated reference. When the reference falls through three consecutive resets, an Indian maker is left carrying inventory bought at one price and sold at another, and the write-down lands in the same quarter as the volume growth it was meant to support. Vraj's finance head describes the past six quarters as a run of profitable operations and unprofitable stock.

The cost base offers no cushion. Chlorine, benzene and toluene derivatives, industrial power at Gujarat's tariff, steam, and the per-kilolitre charge for effluent sent to the estate's common treatment plant together set a variable cost floor that sits above the price a Chinese producer is currently willing to accept. Domestic makers can compete on service, on regulatory paperwork and on proximity. They cannot compete below their own marginal cost.

"Every quarter we tell the board destocking is over, and every quarter the price sheet says something else," said the chief financial officer of a rival unlisted maker in south Gujarat, speaking on the condition that the company not be named.
The qualification clock nobody can skip

What keeps the capex logic alive is the length of the entry process on the other side. A multinational formulator that wants to buy an intermediate from an Indian plant will take samples, run validation batches, audit the site for safety and quality systems, register the source with its own regulators and only then place a commercial order. Depending on the molecule and the destination market, that runs eighteen months to three years.

The corollary is that the plant has to exist before the audit. A customer will not qualify a drawing. Vraj's new block is a multipurpose one, glass lined and Hastelloy reactors on the same floor, cryogenic capability in one train, designed to run campaigns rather than a single product. That flexibility costs more per installed tonne and is the only configuration that lets a company chase qualifications it has not yet won.

Once a source is qualified it is sticky, because switching means repeating the whole exercise. That is the wager: three or four difficult years to buy a position that survives the cycle. Several Gujarat and Maharashtra makers are placing versions of the same bet at the same time, which is itself a risk nobody in the cluster likes to discuss.
Working capital is the real constraint

Ask a promoter in Ankleshwar what keeps him awake and the answer is rarely the price sheet. It is the gap between paying for a container of raw material at sight and collecting from a formulator ninety or a hundred and twenty days after dispatch, with a monsoon in between during which the formulator's own collections stop. Working capital cycles across the sector have stretched by several weeks since the downturn began.

Funding the expansion into that is the hard part. Internal accrual is thin, the promoter family has already put in one round, and a term loan against a plant with no committed offtake is a difficult credit note to write. State industrial incentives help at the margin, and there is no production linked incentive scheme covering most of this chemistry.

"The credit committee is not underwriting this year's operating profit," said a banker at a mid-sized private lender who has appraised three such proposals in the past year. "It is being asked to underwrite a customer list that does not exist yet."
Three things that have to go right

The first is supply discipline abroad. Chinese environmental enforcement and the consolidation of small units in the eastern provinces have tightened supply before, and most Indian projections quietly assume some version of it happens again. The second is diversification of the customer mix, away from crop protection where a bad monsoon anywhere in the world flows straight through, and towards contract manufacturing for pharmaceutical customers with longer horizons.

The third is utilisation. A multipurpose block that runs at a third of nameplate for two years is an expensive way to hold an option. Interest and depreciation begin on commissioning, whether or not the qualification letters arrive, and the same fixed cost that looks modest in a recovery looks ruinous in a flat market.

Vraj's management is candid that the sequencing is uncomfortable.
