The alternative, they argue, is to wait for prices to recover and then begin a three-year qualification cycle from a standing start, by which point the customer will have qualified somebody else. In a cluster where at least two mid-sized units have already gone to lenders for restructuring, that is a defensible position and not a comfortable one.

title: In a shed off the Latehar road, a pilot plant chases battery-grade flake
dek: A small flotation circuit on the Jharkhand graphite belt is testing whether local ore can be lifted to a purity that cell makers will accept.

body.text: The ball mill starts at twenty past five, before there is much light, and for the next hour it is the loudest thing in the valley. The shed that holds it stands off the road between Daltonganj and Latehar, behind a gate with no signboard, and everything inside is the size a chemical engineer would call a demonstration and a mining engineer would call small.

Twenty tonnes of run-of-mine graphite ore go in on a good day. What comes out at the far end of a bank of flotation cells is a grey-black froth that an operator skims off with a paddle when the machine is misbehaving, which is often. The froth is graphite. Almost everything else is not.

India has mined graphite for decades, in Odisha, Jharkhand, Tamil Nadu and Arunachal Pradesh, and has sold most of it into refractories, crucibles, foundry facings and pencils, at prices that reward tonnage rather than purity. The pilot exists because of a different customer. An anode for a lithium-ion cell needs graphite at a purity and a particle shape that nothing in this belt currently produces, and the National Critical Mineral Mission has put money and attention behind finding out whether that can change.
What the froth tells you

The metallurgist running the circuit spends most of the morning looking at the surface of the second cleaner cell. Colour, bubble size and the way the froth breaks tell him whether the reagent dose is right before any laboratory result does. He worked eleven years in an iron ore concentrator in Odisha before this, and says the transition took him a season to accept.

Graphite beneficiation punishes the instinct to grind. In an iron circuit, finer grinding liberates more mineral and is generally good. Here the value sits in large flakes, which command a premium, and aggressive grinding destroys them. The flowsheet is therefore a sequence of gentle stages: grind a little, float, regrind the middlings, float again, six or seven cleaner stages to move the concentrate from the low nineties into the mid nineties as a percentage of fixed carbon.

"Anyone can hit ninety-four per cent if you let them mill it to dust," the metallurgist said, tapping the side of a cell. "The whole job is getting there with the flakes still whole, because the flakes are what pays."

Feed variability is the other problem. The ore arrives from three small pits with different weathering and different silicate content, and blends badly. A quarter of the pilot's running time goes into deliberately feeding single-source campaigns so the team can write a flowsheet a bank will lend against, rather than one that only works on a good day.
Leases the size of a cricket ground

The belt's structure works against scale. Holdings here are small and fragmented, some of them decades old, several of them worked seasonally by operators who sell to traders in Katni and Bhavnagar. Consolidating enough contiguous ground to justify a commercial plant means negotiating with people whose current business, low grade material sold by the truck, is doing fine without a beneficiation plant attached to it.

Around the pilot, the local economy reflects that. Trucks leave loaded with material that will be sorted by hand somewhere else. A transport permit, issued by the district mining office, follows each one. The district mineral foundation has funded a culvert and a stretch of road surface on the approach, which the sarpanch of the nearest panchayat regards as the single tangible thing the mineral economy has delivered in five years.
The step nobody in India has built

Even a clean ninety-six per cent concentrate is not an anode. It has to be micronised, shaped into rounded particles in a process that throws away something close to half the input, and then purified to a level with four nines after the decimal point, either with hydrofluoric acid or in a furnace hot enough to boil off the impurities. Neither route exists at commercial scale in India today.

The acid route is cheaper and brings an effluent stream that no state pollution control board will wave through quickly, and should not. The thermal route needs power at a price that makes the arithmetic difficult. The promoters have talked to two cell makers about offtake and describe the conversations as encouraging and non-committal in equal measure, which is what an anode qualification cycle of two to three years produces.

"They will take our sample, and they will keep buying from China while they test it," said a director of the company that owns the pilot. "That is not bad faith. Nobody starts a gigafactory on a material that has been made in a shed for eight months."
Wages, dust and the road out

About a hundred and eighty people work on the site, most of them engaged through a labour contractor from villages within fifteen kilometres. Wages are paid weekly. Provident fund coverage arrived last year after an inspection, and two of the workers interviewed described the change mainly as a deduction they had to have explained to them.

Graphite dust gets into everything. It settles on the transformer yard, on the mango trees behind the tailings pond and on the collars of everyone coming off shift. Masks are issued. Compliance with wearing them improves visibly whenever a visitor with a notebook is on site, which the safety officer acknowledges without embarrassment.

The mill stops in the early evening. A day's concentrate, perhaps a few hundred kilograms of it, goes into lined drums, and a sample goes to a laboratory in Ranchi and a second one to Hyderabad, because the promoters have learned not to trust a single assay. The answer takes about three weeks. Then the reagent dose changes slightly, and the mill starts again at twenty past five.

title: The regional routes that stopped flying but were never cancelled
dek: Awarded under the connectivity scheme with funding attached, a set of thin routes thinned further and then stopped, leaving staffed airports waiting.

body.text: The terminal at a small airport in western Madhya Pradesh has eight chairs, a working baggage scanner, a fire tender whose water is tested every Monday and a current aerodrome licence. What it has not had since last summer is a scheduled flight.

The route meant to use it, a morning turn to the state capital and back, was awarded three years ago under the regional connectivity scheme with viability gap funding attached to a capped block of seats. It flew for eleven months on a nineteen-seat turboprop, went from daily to three days a week, then to two, then stopped. The award has not formally lapsed. The airport is still staffed.

It is not alone. A reading of award documents from four bidding rounds, monthly performance filings lodged with the implementing agency, and correspondence between two state governments and the civil aviation ministry points at a consistent shape: routes are won in bulk, a share of them never start, a larger share start and quietly stop, and the fixed cost of an operational aerodrome keeps running underneath all of it.
How the funding was meant to work

The economics were meant to be straightforward. An operator bids the subsidy it needs per seat on a capped number of seats, wins exclusivity on the route for three years, and is paid the difference between a capped fare and its bid. The money comes from a levy on other domestic routes, pooled in a trust administered by the ministry, with the concerned state contributing a fifth of the amount, or a tenth in the north east and the hill states. States also cap value added tax on fuel and provide land, security and fire cover.

The design assumed the binding constraint was demand risk. Remove it for three years, the reasoning went, and a thin route would season into a commercial one. On the routes that worked, and there are several, that is broadly what happened. On the ones that did not, demand was never the constraint.
The aircraft that were never there

The most common reason a route stops is that the aeroplane for it does not exist in the operator's fleet. Nineteen and thirty-seat turboprops are a thin global market. The used ones are old, the new ones sit behind long order books, and neither category has much of a maintenance ecosystem in India, so an unscheduled component change can ground an aircraft for weeks while a part clears customs. Two operators that bid across successive rounds were flying fewer than five serviceable aircraft between them when their combined route obligations peaked.

Crew follows the same logic. A type rating on a small turboprop is not a career move for a pilot who intends to fly narrowbodies, and a regional operator cannot pay enough to make it one. One operator's flight operations head said he had trained eleven first officers in two years and lost nine of them, mostly to airlines willing to reimburse the training bond on the candidate's behalf.

"You can subsidise a seat. You cannot subsidise a captain who has already decided he wants to fly jets," said the flight operations head of a regional operator that has held route awards in three rounds.

Airport readiness cuts in the other direction. Several awarded routes were bid on the assumption that a strip would have night landing facilities, a published instrument approach or an extended runway by the time services began. Where the civil works ran late, the operator was left with a schedule that only worked in daylight, which on a single-aircraft rotation means one unserviceability cascades through the entire day.
Penalties that are rarely pressed

The contracts have teeth on paper. An operator that fails to fly the agreed frequency can have its performance guarantee encashed and can be barred from later rounds. Enforcement is softer than the paperwork. Extensions are granted for unserviceability, for airport readiness, for the absence of night operations, for a state's unpaid share. Officials describe the alternative, stripping an award and leaving a town with nothing at all, as politically unavailable in most cases.

The result is a category of route that is neither operating nor cancelled. An airport in that condition cannot be offered to another operator, because the exclusivity is live. It cannot be handed back, because the award stands. It employs a station manager, security staff, firefighters and an air traffic services unit, and it sees a training flight perhaps twice a month.

Two state governments have written asking for either the resumption of services or the release of the route for rebidding. One of those letters, dated more than a year ago, has been acknowledged and not answered. A state civil aviation official said his department continues to budget its share of viability gap funding for routes it knows are not flying, because the alternative is to formally withdraw and forfeit its place in the next round.
What the traffic actually did

Demand, where it existed, went back to the road. In the western Madhya Pradesh district, the surviving connection is an overnight bus or a four-hour drive to a larger airport with jet services. A travel agent in the district town said he sold perhaps forty tickets a month on the flight at its peak, mostly to families visiting relatives and to two pharmaceutical companies with plants nearby, and that the traffic he had built dispersed within a quarter of the last departure.

Route design explains part of the failure. Some awarded pairs connected towns with no historical travel relationship, chosen because they made a bid arithmetic work rather than because anyone wanted to make the journey. Others sat under a fare cap that suited a fifty-minute sector and not the ninety-minute one actually flown, once the routing avoided restricted airspace.

"The scheme did open genuinely new markets, and nobody in the ministry disputes that the failures cluster in identifiable places," said a former official who worked on two of the bidding rounds. "What it never built was a clean way to stop paying for the ones that did not work."

A further round is being prepared. Officials say the terms will lean harder on airport readiness before a route is offered, and on operators demonstrating fleet availability rather than promising it. Neither change reaches the aerodromes already licensed, already staffed and already waiting. At the terminal in western Madhya Pradesh the arrival board is switched on every morning at nine, because the station manager takes the view that switching it off is a decision nobody has authorised him to make.

title: Sarayu Air defers six inductions as engine shop visits stretch past a year
dek: The carrier's capacity plan now turns on how fast grounded aircraft return, and on lessors willing to write short and expensive extensions.

body.text: Eleven of Sarayu Air's aircraft are on the ground, and only three of them are there for reasons the airline can do anything about. The other eight are waiting on engines: removed, shipped, logged into a repair shop somewhere outside India and queued behind everybody else's.

The carrier, a mid-sized operator built around a single narrowbody type and a network that leans on Tier-2 cities, told lessors and lenders this month that it is pushing the induction of six aircraft from this financial year into the next. Management has framed the deferral as a matching exercise rather than a retreat. There is little point taking delivery of airframes, the chief operating officer told an internal briefing, while a third of the existing fleet cannot fly for want of a serviceable engine.

The proximate cause is an inspection programme on a widely used engine family that has pulled powerplants off wing across the industry and filled the world's repair shops. Turnaround times that ran seventy-five to ninety days before the programme are now quoted well past two hundred and fifty, and several Indian operators say the quoted number has itself become unreliable.
The grounded tail problem

A grounded aircraft is not a neutral asset. Lease rentals continue, insurance continues, and the crew rostered against it either flies something else or sits at home on a guarantee. Sarayu has been recovering part of the cost through compensation arrangements with the manufacturer, in a mixture of cash, credit notes and lease of substitute engines, and the airline's finance team says the credit component is worth considerably less than the cash it replaces.

The operational answer has been to shrink the network rather than thin it. Rather than cutting frequencies everywhere, the airline has withdrawn entirely from a handful of stations and concentrated the remaining aircraft on routes that fill in both directions. That protects yield and costs the carrier slots and visibility at airports it may want to return to.

"An airline with a grounded fleet does not have a capacity problem, it has a credibility problem," said a lessor's India representative who has aircraft on lease to three domestic carriers. "The corporate contracts go first, because a travel manager cannot sell an airline that keeps cancelling."
Leases written for another market

Roughly a third of Sarayu's fleet comes up for lease renewal over the next eighteen months, and the terms available are nothing like the ones signed when the aircraft were inducted. Global demand for used narrowbodies has been firm through the delivery slowdown at both large manufacturers, and lessors have been able to reprice.

That leaves the airline choosing between short extensions at high rates, which preserve flexibility and hurt unit cost, and long ones that lock in today's pricing for a decade. Two people involved in the negotiations described the airline as taking short extensions on older tails and pushing for longer terms only where the aircraft is young enough to be worth holding.

Redeliveries complicate the maths further. An aircraft returned to a lessor must meet return conditions on engine life, cabin state and paint, and the cost of meeting them at a maintenance facility with its own queue can rival a year of rentals. Some carriers have concluded it is cheaper to extend an aircraft they do not particularly want.
Where the money is made now

The revenue side has held up better than the fleet has. Fares across the domestic market have been firm because the industry as a whole is short of capacity, which means Sarayu's smaller network is flying fuller and at higher average fares than its business plan assumed. That is a fragile kind of good news, since it reverses the moment the grounded aircraft come back.

Ancillary revenue has become the more durable line. Seat selection, checked baggage, priority boarding, on-board sales and a co-branded credit card now contribute a share of revenue that management describes as approaching the mid teens in percentage terms, up substantially over three years. Cargo is the other lever: belly capacity out of the metros has been in demand, and the airline has been running dedicated cargo loads on late-night sectors where passenger demand is thin.
Crew is the slower constraint

The airline kept hiring pilots through the grounding, which looked expensive at the time and now looks like the least regrettable decision on the list. Type-rated first officers take months to produce, simulator slots in India are scarce enough that operators send cadets abroad, and a command upgrade requires hours that a shrunken network makes harder to accumulate.

Revised flight duty time limitations, phased in by the regulator to lengthen weekly rest and tighten night operations, raise crew requirement per aircraft across the industry. Airlines have argued about the transition timeline. None of them disputes the direction, and every carrier's planning now assumes it needs more pilots per tail than it did three years ago.

"We are training crew for aircraft that are sitting on a taxiway with no engines," said a rostering manager at the carrier, who was not authorised to speak publicly. "It feels absurd in September. It will not feel absurd when the engines come back."

What Sarayu is really buying with the deferral is time to align three schedules it does not control: the repair shop queue, the manufacturer's delivery stream and the pace at which its own crew becomes available. If the engines return before the fares soften, the plan works. If the order is reversed, the airline will be adding capacity into a market that has stopped paying for it.

title: Cool chain, hot floor: a night on the export dock at Bengaluru
dek: Between ten at night and dawn, a perishables terminal moves roses, okra and vaccines onto belly holds against a European customs cut-off.

body.text: The roses come in at half past ten, in cartons stacked five high on a flatbed that has driven three hours down from Hosur, and the first thing anyone does is put a probe into one of them. Six degrees. The floor supervisor writes the number on the airway bill copy and waves the truck toward the cold dock.

This is the export perishables shed at Bengaluru's airport, and from now until roughly four in the morning it is the busiest square of concrete in Karnataka. Nandi Air Cargo Services, the handler that runs this terminal under contract, will build about forty unit load devices tonight. Almost all of them are going into the belly of a passenger aircraft.

The floor is loud and the sequencing is unforgiving. Every consignment has to be weighed, screened, palletised to a contour that will fit a specific hold, documented for customs and plant quarantine, and staged in the right order. Miss the cut-off for the Frankfurt departure and a shipment of cut flowers with a four-day vase life waits eighteen hours in a chamber, losing value the whole time.
The two o'clock cut-off

The clock runs backwards from a departure. Doors close at a fixed time, which sets the last time a loaded pallet can reach the ramp, which sets the screening deadline, which sets the moment the customs entry has to be filed. Every step has a buffer built into it, and every buffer gets eaten on a night when a truck arrives late from a farm gate.

Screening is where the queue forms. Freight moves through X-ray machines and explosive trace detection under the aviation security regime, and a pallet that has been built cannot be screened, so the sequence has to be right the first time. On a heavy night the shift will run every machine on the floor and still watch a consignment miss its flight because it arrived unlabelled and had to be broken down and rebuilt.

"People think the aeroplane is the hard part," the shift supervisor said, standing where he can see both the screening line and the ramp door. "The aeroplane leaves on time. It is the last truck that decides whether we make it."
Belly space and a missing freighter

Most of what leaves Bengaluru at night flies under passengers. Long-haul departures to Europe and the Gulf carry perishables and pharmaceuticals in the lower deck, and the space available depends on how heavy the passenger load is and how much fuel the aircraft is carrying. In the monsoon, when aircraft tanker fuel against weather diversions, the cargo allocation moves without warning.

That makes booking a bet. A forwarder holding two tonnes of okra and drumstick for a London wholesaler books space on two flights, because the first may be cut back at the last minute, and pays a penalty on whichever booking he does not use. Handlers describe a standing queue of shipments that are confirmed on paper and provisional in practice.

"I do not sell my customer a flight, I sell him a week," said a forwarder who has moved flowers out of this shed for eleven seasons. "Which aircraft it goes on is my problem, and some nights it is my loss."

A dedicated freighter would solve much of this, and the terminal's management has been asking for one for years. The arithmetic has never quite closed: strong outbound demand, thin inbound, and a return leg that has to be filled with something. Freighter operators have run seasonal services here and withdrawn them again.
Paperwork at the quarantine window

On the far side of the shed is a counter that most passengers never imagine exists. A plant quarantine officer inspects samples of horticultural consignments and issues the phytosanitary certificate that the importing country's border will demand. Without it a pallet of grapes is a pallet of grapes; with it, it is an admissible shipment.

The officer on duty said the volume of paper has fallen since the process moved onto an electronic single window, and the volume of questions has not. Destination requirements change, sometimes at short notice, and a specification that was acceptable last season may fail this one. Consignments get held. A customs house agent argues, then reworks, then argues again.

The pharmaceutical shipments follow a different discipline entirely. Temperature-controlled containers arrive pre-conditioned, sit in a monitored chamber, and are supposed to spend as little time as possible on the open apron, which in Bengaluru in the pre-monsoon months means the tarmac itself is the risk. The handler runs a covered dolly for those pallets and treats any excursion in the data logger as an incident to be documented.
Wages, forklifts and the six-hour turn

About two hundred and sixty people work this shift. A little over half are on the handler's own rolls; the rest come through two manpower contractors, doing the loading, palletising and net work that the floor runs on. Forklift operators are the scarce skill, and the terminal has been running a training scheme because the ones it trains keep leaving for warehouse jobs in the industrial belt that pay similarly and finish at six in the evening.

The canteen opens at one in the morning. There is a rest room with a television and, at the far end, a wall of laminated sheets showing correct lifting technique in three languages. A loader in his second year said the work is steady and the nights are the problem; his family in a village near Kolar sees him awake on Sundays and asleep for most of the rest.

By a quarter past four the last pallet for the Frankfurt service is on a dolly train and the floor empties out in stages. The cold chambers hum. A supervisor closes out the shift on a terminal that still, for reasons nobody can explain, requires the tonnage to be entered twice. Outside, the first trucks of the day shift are already waiting at the gate with tomorrow night's roses.

title: Auction fatigue sets in as commercial coal blocks return unsold
dek: Bidders are walking away from blocks with thin geology and no rail link, forcing a rethink of what goes on the block.

body.text: The tranche closed much as the previous two had. Of the mines offered for commercial mining in the latest round, a little under half drew a single qualified bid, and several drew none at all. Officials in the coal ministry describe the pattern in flatter language than the press notes do. The blocks that were always going to sell have sold. What is left on the shelf is geologically thinner, further from a railhead, or sitting under forest that nobody wants to be the first to clear.

For four years the auction programme has carried the weight of two separate ambitions: cutting thermal coal imports, and ending a state monopoly that had stood since nationalisation in 1973. On the first count the numbers have moved. On the second, the arithmetic is less flattering. Hundreds of blocks have been allotted since commercial mining opened. Only a modest fraction of them are producing, and the distance between those two figures has become the central fact of the sector.

That gap is now shaping the auction calendar itself. Two rounds have been re-notified with revised reserve prices. Others have quietly dropped blocks that failed twice. A senior official in a state mining directorate said his department had stopped forecasting revenue from three allotted blocks in its budget documents, because the developers had not yet filed a mining plan.
What bidders are actually pricing

The bid variable in a commercial auction is a revenue share, quoted as a percentage above a floor. In the early rounds, aggressive bidders quoted premiums in the high double digits, on the expectation that e-auction realisations would stay near the peaks of the import-price spike. Those realisations have since come off. A developer who quoted a forty per cent share against a market that has normalised is running a mine whose margin now depends on cost control it has not yet demonstrated.

The second variable is time. Bank guarantees are staged against milestones, and every quarter a block spends in clearance limbo is a quarter of guarantee cost with no offsetting revenue. Consultants who advise bidders say they now build a two-year clearance assumption into the base case and a four-year one into the downside, and that the downside case is winning more often than it used to.

"A block is not an asset until it has a siding and a stage-two forest clearance; before that it is a liability with a bank guarantee attached," said a mine development consultant who has worked on bids in five tranches.
The evacuation bottleneck

Coal that cannot move is coal that cannot be sold, and the constraint has shifted from the pithead to the corridor. Rail capacity in the Talcher and Ib valley belts has been expanded, but the first-mile links from individual mines to the trunk lines remain the developer's responsibility. Those links cross private land, canals and, frequently, a village that has already given land once.

The alternative is road transport to the nearest siding, which works at small volumes and stops working at large ones. Trucking a substantial share of a mine's annual output over district roads adds cost per tonne, invites the pollution board's attention, and makes the mine an unpopular neighbour. Several private operators have run at a fraction of rated capacity for precisely this reason, unable to justify the higher production their bid assumed.

The ministry has pushed a mechanised first-mile programme, with silos and closed conveyors replacing open loading. The equipment works. The financing is the difficulty: a conveyor corridor is a fixed asset with a payback measured against a mine whose reserve life is itself under negotiation.
Clearances that outlast the capex plan

Environmental and forest clearance remains the longest line item on any block's timeline. Developers describe a sequence in which the terms of reference arrive quickly, the public hearing is scheduled and then deferred, and the district administration waits for a state-level committee that meets when its quorum permits. None of these steps is unreasonable on its own. Stacked, they consume years.

"We had our funding tied up and our contractor mobilised, and we spent eleven months waiting for one committee's minutes to be uploaded," said a project director at a private miner developing a block in central India.

There is a policy answer on offer, and it is contested. One school inside the ministry wants blocks pre-cleared before auction, so that the state absorbs the clearance risk and the bidder pays for it in the premium. The counter-argument is fiscal: pre-clearing a block the state may never sell is money spent on nothing, and the environment ministry has shown little appetite for issuing clearances to a hypothetical operator.
The transition question nobody has costed

Running alongside the auction file is a slower one. Several coalfields in Jharkhand and West Bengal have mines approaching the end of economic life, and the districts around them have no second industry. State planning departments have begun commissioning transition studies, mostly funded by multilateral lenders, and the studies keep reaching the same conclusion: the fiscal dependence of these districts on royalties and district mineral foundation funds runs deeper than the employment dependence.

That matters for the auction programme, because a state that loses royalty from a closing mine has every incentive to push a new block into production quickly, whatever its clearance status. The pressure runs in the opposite direction from the environmental process, and the two meet on the district collector's desk.

For now, the stated position is that the calendar continues. A revised tranche is expected before the end of the financial year, with a smaller number of blocks and, officials indicate, lower floor prices on the least attractive of them. Whether that clears the shelf or simply moves the discount around is the question the next round will answer.

title: Mine operators seek to reprice contracts as stripping ratios climb
dek: Heavier overburden and softer e-auction realisations have pushed developer-operator contracts signed three years ago into renegotiation.

body.text: When Damodar Mining and Minerals signed its mine developer and operator contract for a block in the Ib valley, the arithmetic was straightforward. The contractor would remove overburden and raise coal at a fixed rate per tonne, escalated annually against a diesel and wage index, and the miner would sell into an e-auction market then running well above notified prices. Three years on, both halves of that sentence have moved.

The company is in its second round of discussions with the contractor over the rate. It is not alone. Lawyers who paper these contracts say renegotiation requests have become routine across privately held blocks, driven by two forces that arrived together: a stripping ratio rising faster than the mine plan assumed, and auction realisations drifting back towards the notified price.
Neither force is a surprise on its own. Together they compress a margin that was never wide.
Why the overburden number moved

A stripping ratio is the volume of waste rock that must be moved for each tonne of coal recovered. It is estimated from exploration boreholes, and in blocks explored to a lower confidence category the estimate can be optimistic. Developers say the ratios encountered in the first benches of several recently opened mines have come in above the geological report, sometimes materially.

The cost consequence is direct. Overburden removal is the single largest line in an opencast mine's operating cost, and it scales with volume moved rather than with coal produced. A ratio that rises by one full unit can add a double-digit percentage to cost per tonne, and it does so before the first rake leaves the siding.
"The contract was priced on a mine plan; we are operating on a different orebody," said a contracts manager at a mining services firm that runs three opencast blocks in eastern India.

Contractors have their own escalation problem. Heavy earthmoving fleets are financed, and interest costs on that equipment have not fallen. Skilled dumper operators command wages set by a competitive market across infrastructure and mining. Where the escalation index in a contract lags actual wage movement, the contractor absorbs the difference until it cannot.
The revenue side stopped cooperating

E-auction premiums over notified price were the industry's cushion through the import-price spike. Buyers who could not secure linkage coal bid aggressively, and privately mined coal cleared at a comfortable spread. That spread has narrowed as supply from state and private producers has come on together, and as imported coal has become cheaper at the western ports.

For a commercial block, the squeeze is sharper than for a captive one. A captive developer feeds its own plant and values the coal at avoided cost. A commercial miner sells into the market and pays a revenue share on the realisation. When the realisation falls, the share falls with it, but the operating cost does not.

Traders describe a market in which the grade discount has widened as well. Buyers with washeries or blending capacity will take lower-grade coal at a price. Buyers without will not take it at any price they consider sensible. Producers whose output has slipped a grade band against the declared specification are discovering how thin that market is.
What renegotiation actually looks like

The contracts being reopened rarely change headline rates. Instead the parties adjust the structure: a separate rate band for overburden above an agreed ratio, a revised escalation index with a fuel component marked to actual purchases, or a volume commitment that gives the contractor fleet certainty in exchange for a lower unit price.

Lenders are reading the same documents. A term loan against a mine assumes a cost curve, and a renegotiated contract changes it. Bankers who have financed two or three of these blocks say they now ask for the contractor's own equipment financing schedule as part of the annual review, on the theory that a contractor in distress is a mine that stops.
"We used to underwrite the coal price and treat the contractor as a given; now we underwrite the contractor," said a lender at a private bank that has funded several block acquisitions.

Some of that fleet is leaving the sector. Two mid-sized earthmoving contractors have redeployed equipment to road and irrigation projects, where payment cycles are slower but the volume risk sits with the client. A mine that loses its contractor mid-contract faces a re-tender in a shallower market, and the replacement bid is rarely cheaper.

The wider consequence is a slower ramp. Blocks expected to reach rated capacity within three years of first production are settling at a plateau below it, with the developer preferring a stable, lower volume at a defensible cost over a stretch target that requires more fleet than the contract will fund. In a sector whose central promise was faster private supply, that plateau is the number worth watching.

title: On Korba's haul roads, the coalfield's growth is measured in dust
dek: Contract truckers, a resettled colony and a district hospital's chest clinic map the human ledger of a coalfield still expanding.

body.text: The queue starts before first light. By twenty to six the tippers are three deep at the weighbridge outside the mine gate, engines idling, their drivers standing in the road with tea in steel glasses. The road surface here is black and slightly greasy, a mixture of spilled fines and the water a tanker sprays twice a shift, and it holds the shape of every tyre that has crossed it.

Korba's mines have grown steadily for two decades, and the town has grown around the logistics rather than around the mining. The men in the queue are not employed by the mine. They drive for transport contractors holding sub-contracts under a larger haulage tender, and their pay is a per-trip rate against a fuel allowance that everyone in the queue can recite from memory.

What has changed recently is not the work but its rhythm. Mechanised first-mile evacuation, the conveyors and silos the coal ministry has pushed to cut road movement, has begun arriving at some of the larger pits. Where it lands, the trip count falls.
A per-trip economy

Ask a driver what a good day looks like and the answer is a number of trips, not a number of hours. Four is respectable on the short lead to the siding. Two is what a day of breakdown and queueing produces, and two does not cover the instalment on a truck bought against a hypothecation loan.

The owner-drivers are the exposed ones. A man who drives someone else's tipper takes a daily wage and goes home. A man who has financed his own carries a fixed monthly outflow against a variable trip count, and his cushion is measured in weeks.

"When the conveyor came up at the other pit, the fleet from that side moved onto our lead, and the queue at our weighbridge doubled," said an owner-driver who has hauled from the same mine for eleven years.

The transport contractors describe the same shift from the other end. Their tenders are volume-based, and where a mine mechanises, the tendered volume shrinks at the next renewal. Two contractors in the district said they had begun bidding instead for overburden haulage inside the pit, which pays better per hour and requires heavier, costlier trucks.
The village that moved and the one that did not

Eight kilometres from the gate is a resettlement colony built when the mine's boundary was last extended. It has a school building, a water tank on a steel frame, and rows of two-room houses laid out on a grid. What it does not have, its residents say, is the thing they gave up: land that produced something.

Compensation in these cases is settled in two currencies, cash and employment, and the second generates the longer dispute. A job against land is allotted per acre surrendered above a threshold, and families whose holdings were divided among brothers before acquisition frequently fall below it. A retired schoolteacher in the colony keeps a folder of the correspondence: an application, three acknowledgements, and a rejection citing a revenue record the family says it never saw.

A kilometre further, a hamlet that was not acquired sits within the blast-notification radius. Its residents get a siren and a text message before each blast. They have asked, through the panchayat, for either acquisition or a wider buffer, and have received neither.
What the chest clinic sees

At the district hospital the pulmonology outpatient department fills on Tuesdays. The clinical picture that walks in is familiar to any doctor in a mining belt: chronic cough, breathlessness on exertion, a chest film with the diffuse markings that suggest years of particulate exposure. Formal occupational-disease certification, which would open a compensation claim, requires an exposure history the patient often cannot document, because he worked for a contractor no longer traceable.

"The diagnosis is the easy part; proving where the man breathed the dust for fifteen years is what the file turns on," said a physician who runs the outpatient chest clinic at a government hospital in the coalfield.

The state pollution control board monitors ambient particulate levels at fixed stations, and the readings around Korba are public and consistently high in the dry months. Enforcement, where it happens, takes the form of directions to increase water spraying and to metal the haul roads. Both help. Neither addresses a fleet that runs uncovered because covering a tipper costs a few minutes per trip in an economy counted in trips.
A transition nobody in the queue is planning for

Chhattisgarh's mining districts are among those named in the transition studies now circulating between state planning departments and multilateral lenders. The studies talk about reskilling, about solar manufacturing on reclaimed overburden dumps, about tourism on flooded voids. Read from the weighbridge queue, they are documents about a decade that has not begun.

The drivers' own planning horizon is the loan schedule. Several said they expected to sell the truck within three years, either to a smaller operator working the shortest leads or to a scrap dealer. None described a plan that involved leaving the district. The town, as one of them put it, has only ever had one employer, and it has never called itself that.

title: Satellite broadband's pricing question returns to the regulator's desk
dek: With administrative assignment settled in law, the fight has narrowed to what satellite operators pay, for how long, and on what base.

body.text: The principle was settled in the statute. Spectrum for satellite-based services would be assigned administratively rather than auctioned, a departure from the position India has held for terrestrial mobile spectrum since the courts made auctions the default more than a decade ago. What was not settled, and what has occupied the regulator for the better part of a year, is the price.

The consultation now in its second round asks a narrow set of questions with wide consequences. Should the charge be a percentage of adjusted gross revenue or a fee per megahertz? Should it differ between geostationary satellites and low-earth-orbit constellations? Should a spectrum charge apply at all to capacity a foreign operator sells wholesale to an Indian licensee? And how long should an assignment run before it is revisited?

Terrestrial operators have filed. Satellite applicants have filed. The two sets of submissions do not agree on a single material question, and the regulator's difficulty is that both sides argue from the same principle of a level playing field to opposite conclusions.
Two definitions of parity

The terrestrial argument is straightforward. Mobile operators bought spectrum at auction, financed the purchase over long tenors, and carry the resulting debt on their balance sheets. A satellite operator receiving comparable spectrum administratively, at a revenue-linked charge, enters the same broadband market with a materially lower fixed cost. Parity, on this reading, means a charge calibrated so that the effective cost per unit of delivered capacity is not wildly different.

The satellite argument starts elsewhere. A constellation is a shared global asset. Indian revenue is a fraction of its traffic, the spectrum is coordinated internationally rather than held exclusively, and the addressable market is by definition the part of the country terrestrial networks have not found economic to serve. Charging as though the operator held exclusive national spectrum, on this reading, prices the service out of the geographies it exists to cover.

"Both sides want parity, and both mean something different by it; the regulator has to pick one definition and then defend it," said a telecom policy adviser who has drafted submissions for operators on both sides of the question.
The rural obligation in the fine print

Buried in the consultation is a question that may matter more than the headline rate: whether satellite licensees will carry a rural service obligation, and in what form. Terrestrial operators contribute to the universal service fund through a levy on revenue. The fund has historically underspent, and BharatNet, its largest beneficiary, has been through more than one revision of model and timeline.

Some officials see satellite capacity as a way to reach the last few thousand gram panchayats where fibre has been laid and does not work, or has not been laid at all. That would imply a subsidised terminal, a defined service level, and procurement through the state. Applicants are cautious about the terminal subsidy in particular, because a subsidised terminal creates an obligation to service it for years at a price the operator does not set.

Enterprise demand, by contrast, is immediate. Mining companies, offshore operators, shipping lines and disaster-management agencies want managed connectivity at sites where laying fibre is impossible. That market can absorb a high spectrum charge. A consumer market in a hill district cannot, and a single charge applied to both will decide which of the two the industry actually builds for.
Gateways, landing rights and the security file

Alongside pricing sits a set of conditions that operators consider settled and the security establishment does not. Traffic originating in India must be routed through a gateway inside the country. Lawful interception must be available at that gateway. Terminals must be geo-fenced, so that a device sold for use in one location cannot be carried across a border and used there.

These are engineering requirements with commercial consequences. A national gateway requirement multiplies the ground infrastructure a constellation must build, and geo-fencing at terminal level requires a control layer the operator must maintain and the state must be able to audit.

"The security annexure is not a formality; it is a capital expenditure line and an operating commitment, and it belongs inside the pricing discussion rather than after it," said a former licensing official now advising a satellite applicant.
What happens after the recommendation

The regulator's recommendations are not binding. The department may accept them, refer them back, or accept them with changes, and the interval between a recommendation and a decision has stretched in previous spectrum matters. Applicants who have cleared security clearances and have terminals in a warehouse are running pilots in the meantime under experimental authorisations that do not permit commercial billing.

The commercial cost of delay falls unevenly. A global constellation can wait, since India is one market among many. An Indian licensee that has signed distribution agreements and hired a field-support team cannot. Two such firms have already redeployed staff to enterprise VSAT work, which is licensed, priced and unglamorous, and which pays now.

Officials familiar with the file expect the eventual charge to land as a percentage of adjusted gross revenue with a floor per megahertz, a structure that gives the exchequer a minimum and gives operators a variable cost in the early years. Whether that floor is set at a level a consumer terminal in Arunachal Pradesh can carry is the part nobody will commit to in advance.

title: Densification bills come due at India's tower companies
dek: Small cells cost more per site and earn less per tenant than macro towers, and the infrastructure providers are financing the gap.

body.text: Ashwath Infratel's site count has risen every quarter for three years. Its revenue per site has not. That divergence, which the company's own disclosures describe in the neutral language of tenancy mix, is the clearest available summary of what 5G has done to the tower business in India.

The macro tower model was elegant. Build a tall steel structure, put a generator and a battery bank at its base, and rent space on it to two or three operators who each pay a full rent for their antennas. The marginal tenant costs almost nothing to add and drops nearly all of its rent to operating profit. Tenancy ratio was the number that mattered, and everyone in the industry knew it.

Densification breaks that model in a specific way. A 5G small cell mounted on a street pole serves a fraction of the area of a macro site and costs a fraction as much to build. It also earns a fraction of the rent. What it does not do is carry three tenants.
The tenancy arithmetic stops working

Small cells are, in practice, single-tenant assets. Their placement is dictated by one operator's coverage hole, and the pole, the power connection and the fibre drop are engineered around that operator's radio. A second tenant would need a different sector orientation and would rarely find the same location useful.

That converts an infrastructure business with operating leverage into something closer to build-to-suit contracting. The provider funds the site, the operator pays a rent that amortises it over a contracted term, and the return depends on the term holding. Providers have responded by pushing for longer lock-ins and higher exit penalties, which operators under their own capital discipline are resisting.

"On a macro site we were selling space; on a small cell we are selling a financed asset with a service wrapper, and those are different businesses with different balance sheets," said a chief financial officer at an infrastructure provider operating in four circles.
Fibre is the real capital expenditure

The steel is not the expensive part. Backhaul is. Every small cell needs a fibre connection with the capacity and latency that 5G traffic assumes, and in Indian cities that means trenching through municipal roads under a right-of-way regime that varies by ward, let alone by state.

The Telecommunications Act and the associated right-of-way rules were meant to standardise this, with a single window, a defined timeline and deemed approval if the authority does not respond. Implementation has been uneven. Municipal bodies that derive meaningful revenue from restoration charges have not moved quickly to a lower standardised fee, and some have added conditions that function as the old charge under a new name.

The practical effect is that fibre progress in a city is a function of that city's administration rather than of the operator's plan. Providers who have laid aggressively in one metro have paused in another with a comparable subscriber base, purely on permission throughput.
What the operators are willing to pay for

On the demand side, operators are buying selectively. Densification spending is concentrated in high-traffic urban pockets where a measurable capacity constraint exists, and in enterprise campuses where a private network contract funds the build. Blanket urban densification of the sort the equipment vendors' roadmaps assumed is not being purchased.

Monetisation is the reason. Consumer 5G in India has been sold largely as an unmetered upgrade on an existing tariff, and the tariff repair that followed the last price move has improved average revenue per user without anyone attributing it specifically to 5G. An operator asked to fund a site whose revenue cannot be isolated will fund fewer of them.

"Nobody in this industry can point to a rupee of incremental consumer revenue and say it came from the small cell we built last quarter," said a network planning head at a telecom operator, describing his own capital committee's standing objection.
Consolidation, again

The segment has consolidated once already, and bankers expect another round. The candidates are mid-sized providers with a few thousand sites, no fibre of their own, and a customer concentration that leaves them negotiating against a buyer who knows their cost base. Their asset is the site licence and the power connection, and both are worth more inside a larger portfolio.

A slower structural change is under way as well, in which municipal and state bodies begin monetising their own street furniture directly. A city that rents out its poles at a published rate removes a layer from the chain. Two urban local bodies have floated such policies. Neither has awarded at scale yet, but the infrastructure providers have read the drafts closely.

For now the segment's reported numbers hold up, because macro rentals still carry the portfolio and energy pass-through arrangements have stabilised. The pressure shows a layer down, in the mix of new sites added and in the lengthening gap between capital spent and revenue recognised. That gap is what the next two years will settle.

title: Marked connected: a village link that exists mainly in the ledger
dek: Records show the gram panchayat online. The equipment cupboard tells a different story, and the gap has an accounting explanation.

body.text: The equipment sits in a steel cupboard in the corner of a gram panchayat office in eastern Uttar Pradesh, behind a padlock whose key the secretary keeps in his shirt pocket. Inside are an optical network terminal, a small router, a battery, and a layer of dust that has been undisturbed long enough to have taken the shape of the shelf. The power light is off. It has been off, the secretary says, since some point during the monsoon.
In the central dashboard that tracks the national rural broadband programme, this panchayat is connected. It has been connected, on paper, for more than two years.

The discrepancy is not a scandal in the sense of missing money. It is something duller and more durable: a definition. The programme's completion metric is the laying of fibre to the panchayat building and the commissioning of equipment at both ends. Keeping that equipment powered, repaired and in service is a separate contract, separately funded, and in this block it has been between vendors for longer than anyone can precisely date.
What connected means in the file

Three different records describe this village's connectivity, and all three are accurate within their own terms. The construction record shows fibre laid and spliced, with a joint at the block headquarters and a drop to the panchayat. The commissioning record shows a link tested and handed over, with a signed acceptance. The service record, maintained by whoever holds the current operations and maintenance contract, shows uptime.

The first two are permanent facts. The third is a live measurement, and it is the one that stops being reported when a contract lapses. A district official who oversees the programme locally said uptime reporting from several blocks had gone silent during a transition between agencies, and that silence in the system is not the same thing as a recorded outage.

"There is no field in the form for the vendor having left and nobody having taken over, so the last known status simply stays on the screen," said an official in the district IT cell who has been asked to reconcile the figures twice.
The last hundred metres, and the electricity bill

Where links do fail, the causes are mundane and repetitive. A road-widening contractor cuts the duct and the splice takes weeks. A pole-mounted drop comes down in a storm. Most often the equipment simply loses power: the panchayat building runs on a domestic tariff, the bill is paid from a fund with its own approval cycle, and a disconnection notice is easier to ignore than a broken fibre.

Battery backup was specified in the original design, and batteries have a service life. In several offices visited across two blocks, the backup unit had failed and had not been replaced, because replacement is an operating expense and the operating contract is the one that lapsed.

The block's own count, kept on a register rather than a dashboard, put working links at roughly half of those commissioned when it was last updated. The register is not a formal record and is not reported upward. It exists because a block development officer wanted a number he could rely on when a village complained.

The consequence lands on the services that were meant to justify the network. The common service centre operator, who runs the village's Aadhaar updates, certificate applications and banking correspondent terminal, has moved his work to a mobile hotspot. He pays for the data himself and passes the cost into the fee he charges. Nobody has told him to stop.
Why the numbers keep improving anyway

At state level the programme's reported coverage has continued to rise, and the rise is real in the sense that fibre keeps being laid. The revised implementation model, which shifts more responsibility to a concessionaire carrying a longer service obligation, is designed precisely to close the gap between built and working. Where it has been rolled out, officials say maintenance response has improved.

The rollout is staggered, though, and the blocks built earliest under the older model are the ones most likely to sit in the maintenance gap. That is an unfortunate ordering. The villages that have had fibre the longest have had it working the least recently.
"We are not measuring the same thing we are announcing, and everyone in the chain knows it," said a former project engineer who worked on the earlier phase in two eastern states.
A fix that is mostly administrative

The people closest to it describe remedies that require no new technology. Report uptime by default and treat a silent node as down rather than as last known good. Fund the electricity connection for panchayat network equipment from the same head as the equipment, so that a routine bill cannot take a village offline. Give the panchayat secretary a working escalation number instead of a helpline that routes to the state capital.

None of these are in dispute. They are simply nobody's single responsibility, spread as they are across a central programme, a state implementing agency, a district administration and a village body with no technical staff. In the panchayat office, the secretary has his own summary of the position, which is that the cupboard is locked, the key is in his pocket, and nobody has come for it in a long time.

title: Front-of-pack labelling sets off a quiet reformulation cycle
dek: Star ratings are not final yet, but sugar and sodium are already coming out of recipes, and contract manufacturers are carrying the cost.

body.text: The labels have not changed yet. The recipes have. Across the packaged foods industry, product development teams have spent the past several quarters running reformulation trials against a rule that is not yet in force, on the working assumption that it will be. The Food Safety and Standards Authority of India has moved through successive drafts of a front-of-pack nutrition labelling requirement, and the version the industry expects would put an indicator on the front of every pack, derived from sugar, sodium and saturated fat content.

Companies are not waiting for the final text, because reformulation is slow and packaging is slower. Cutting sugar in a biscuit changes its browning, its texture and its shelf life. Cutting sodium in an extruded snack changes taste and narrows the microbial safety margin. Each change requires stability trials, sensory panels and, frequently, a new supplier for a functional ingredient that has to do the work the removed one was doing.

The result is a reformulation cycle running quietly ahead of the regulation, with most of its cost sitting where the consumer never looks: in third-party manufacturing units, ingredient suppliers and packaging converters.
Where the cost actually sits

A large share of India's packaged food is made under contract, in units clustered around locations that once carried excise advantages, in Himachal Pradesh, Uttarakhand, Assam and Sikkim. Those units are paid a conversion charge per tonne against a fixed recipe and a fixed process. A recipe change means trial batches that produce no saleable output, a line cleaned and reset, and minimum order quantities of a new ingredient that the unit must hold on its own account.

Brand owners generally pay for the ingredient. The line time is more often absorbed, because the contract manufacturer's leverage is limited and the alternative is losing the volume altogether. Plant heads in the Baddi belt describe a year in which trial runs have taken a visible share of scheduled capacity without producing a single case for sale.
"We have run the same biscuit four ways this year for one customer, and none of the four has gone commercial yet," said a plant head at a contract manufacturing unit in the Baddi industrial area.
The scale is the whole argument

The technical fight is over thresholds and the basis of measurement. Industry submissions have pushed for a per-serve basis, arguing that a rating computed on a hundred grams penalises products nobody eats a hundred grams of. Public health groups have pushed back, noting that serving size is declared by the manufacturer and has a history of shrinking whenever it becomes inconvenient.

The second argument is about comparability across categories. A scale calibrated to work for a breakfast cereal, a fruit drink, a namkeen and a cooking oil will be generous to at least one of them. Nutritionists on the drafting side accept the point and argue that a scale which is directionally right beats a label nobody reads.

There is a quieter commercial concern the industry raises less publicly. A front-of-pack indicator makes products comparable at a glance in a way an ingredient list never did, and comparability at a glance favours whoever reformulates first. Several companies have concluded on that basis that moving early is the defensive play rather than the virtuous one.
What a label change costs a small brand

For a large company, artwork revision is a project. For a small one it is a write-off. Regional brands print packaging film in long runs to bring the unit price down, and a converter's economic minimum can represent many months of a small brand's requirement. A rule that changes the front of the pack strands that inventory where it sits.

Converters expect a spike in short-run demand followed by a slump, and are wary of adding capacity for it. Legal metrology declarations, which govern quantity and price display, sit on the same panel, so any change to one usually forces a redesign of the whole.

"The film in my customer's warehouse is not obsolete until the notification says it is, and the day after that it is scrap," said a director at a flexible packaging converter supplying regional food brands in western India.
The claims file is moving faster

While labelling grinds through consultation, enforcement on claims has moved. The Central Consumer Protection Authority has issued guidelines on misleading advertisement and on dark patterns in online retail, and notices have gone to sellers over health claims, drip pricing and interfaces that make a subscription hard to cancel. Consumer companies now route campaign copy through legal review at a stage where it used to go straight to the agency.

The most exposed claims are the comparative and the implied. A pack that says no added sugar while carrying a fruit concentrate, or one that markets a fortified variant on a benefit the evidence does not support, is a straightforward file for a regulator to open. Brand teams have begun retiring phrasing that survived a decade unchallenged.
What it looks like on the shelf

The retail consequence will show up online first. Quick commerce and ecommerce platforms already filter by category and price, and a structured nutrition indicator gives them another filter to sell against. A brand that rates poorly does not disappear; it loses the default position in a search result, which in a ten-minute basket amounts to nearly the same thing.

In physical trade the effect will be slower and probably smaller. Kirana purchase is habitual, and the shopkeeper's recommendation carries more weight than the front of a pack. Even so, distributors in two states said brand teams had begun asking them to clear old artwork faster than usual, which is generally the first sign that a rule is close.

title: A distribution network built for kirana stores meets the ten-minute shelf
dek: Quick commerce has taken the highest-margin urban baskets, and consumer companies are rebuilding a channel designed for another decade.

body.text: Trikaya Consumer Ltd reaches something over a million outlets through a distributor network it spent four decades building, and until recently that network was the company's most defensible asset. A rival could copy a formulation and outspend a media plan. Replicating a stockist in every district, each carrying working capital and a delivery van, took a generation. That defence is now being tested by a channel that does not use stockists at all.

Quick commerce platforms buy centrally, hold inventory in dark stores placed inside dense urban catchments, and deliver in minutes. For a consumer company the channel is attractive in the way any large account is attractive, and risky for the same reason. It consolidates purchasing power that was previously spread across thousands of independent buyers who competed with one another rather than with the brand.

The company's answer, described in its own investor communication as a distribution transformation, is really an attempt to settle two questions at once: what the traditional channel is now for, and who pays for it.
The mix problem beneath the growth

Headline urban growth still looks healthy, because platform volumes are additive at first. The composition is the difficulty. Platforms sell disproportionately in larger pack sizes and premium variants, which is where the gross margin sits, and they sell them in exactly the metro pin codes where the traditional distributor earned the margin that funded his service to weaker outlets.

A distributor's economics are a spread on a portfolio. The fast-moving premium lines pay for the van, the salesman and the credit extended to small shops. Take those lines out of his territory and the remaining portfolio will not support the same infrastructure, which is how a company ends up with falling service levels in the outlets least able to absorb them.

"The platform took the top twenty per cent of my throughput and left me the bottom eighty, and my costs did not move at all," said a distributor in a western metro who has handled the company's lines for nineteen years.
Rewriting the trade terms

The immediate lever is margin structure, and it is contested. Distributor bodies have argued for years that the difference between the price a platform pays and the price a stockist pays amounts to differential treatment of channels selling to the same consumer. Companies reply that the two transactions are not comparable, since a platform takes central delivery, pays on a defined cycle and returns almost nothing.

What companies have actually done is quieter. Several have introduced pack sizes and variants exclusive to a channel, so that a direct price comparison between the platform and the neighbourhood shop becomes difficult to make. Others have moved to a service-based distributor margin, paying for outlet coverage and merchandising rather than simply for turnover.

Neither approach settles the underlying question. A separate pack architecture raises manufacturing complexity and inventory risk, and a service-based margin requires a measurement system the distributor has to be persuaded to accept.
Rural is the other half of the answer

The strategic counterweight is rural distribution, where quick commerce does not reach and is unlikely to soon. Companies have been extending van routes and appointing sub-stockists in smaller towns, on the argument that incremental outlets there are cheap relative to the cost of defending a metro basket.

The constraint is demand rather than reach. Rural volume tracks the agricultural cycle, rural wage rates and the timing of transfers, and a strong urban quarter can mask a flat rural one for a while. Companies that leaned on rural expansion to hold volume growth have found that outlets get added faster than throughput per outlet rises.
"We can open the town in a quarter; making the shop sell a second carton a month takes a year and a media budget," said a regional sales manager at a packaged foods company covering central India.
What the finance function is watching

On the profit and loss statement the visible line is trade spend, which has been rising as companies fund platform visibility alongside conventional trade schemes. Listing charges, banner placement and platform-funded discounts sit in different buckets from a wholesaler's scheme, and they behave differently, because a platform's promotional slot is priced in an auction and a kirana scheme is not.

On the balance sheet, receivable days from platform accounts run longer than from distributors who paid on delivery or against a short credit line. A company shifting a meaningful share of urban volume onto a handful of accounts is also concentrating its credit exposure, which is a question the treasury asks and the sales function tends not to.

None of this amounts to an argument that the traditional channel is finished. It reaches parts of the market nothing else does, and the companies rebuilding around it know that. The open question is whether a network designed to push volume can be repurposed into one that mainly provides coverage, and at what margin its members will agree to stay.

title: In a Nanded godown, the beat plan is being redrawn one shop at a time
dek: A distributor's salesmen, a shrinking order book and a wholesaler two districts away show what channel disruption looks like from the floor.

body.text: The shutter goes up a little after seven, and for the next hour the godown on the edge of Nanded is a loading operation. Cartons of detergent, tea, biscuits and shampoo sachets come off a stack that reaches the ceiling and go into three tempos parked nose-out in the lane. The distributor, who has held these agencies for two decades, works from a printed beat plan and a phone that does not stop ringing.

A beat plan is the week reduced to geography. Each salesman is assigned a set of streets for a given day, and the assumption behind the document is that a shop visited on Tuesday will order enough to last until the next Tuesday. That assumption is the thing currently under strain, and the plan on the desk has been redrawn twice this year.

The reason is not a competitor's brand. It is a wholesaler in a larger town two districts away, a dark store that opened near the college area, and a set of shopkeepers who have started ordering smaller quantities more often.
The order that keeps getting smaller

The salesman's problem is measured in lines and in value. A productive call used to mean eight or ten stock-keeping units and an order the shopkeeper would take three or four days to sell through. Now the same shopkeeper takes four lines and asks him to come back on Friday, because his cash is tied up and he can restock from a nearby wholesaler if he runs short.

For the distributor this is worse than a lost sale. His cost per call is fixed, and it now buys a smaller order. His delivery cost per case rises for the same reason, and the schemes he passes on are calculated against volumes his outlets have stopped reaching. He has responded by lengthening some beats and merging others, which means every shop is now visited slightly less often than it was.

"My salesman is not selling less because the shop sells less; he is selling less because the shop has learned to buy weekly instead of monthly," said the distributor, going through the previous day's call reports.
The wholesaler two districts away

Sitting behind the retail beat is a parallel trade that companies formally discourage and practically depend on. A large wholesaler in a bigger town buys at a scheme-heavy price, sells onward to retailers outside his own territory, and undercuts the local distributor on exactly the fast-moving lines that make the beat viable in the first place.

Every distributor in the region can name the sources. Enforcement is theoretically the brand's responsibility, and in practice it is inconsistent, because the wholesaler's volume shows up in somebody else's target. Two of the agencies in this godown have had their territories redefined in the past three years, which the distributor treats as an acknowledgement of the problem rather than a solution to it.
What the shopkeepers say

In the market lane, a kirana owner who has run the same counter for thirty years keeps a notebook of customer credit and a smartphone with three ordering apps on it. He does not think the apps will replace him. He thinks they have taken the customer who used to buy the large pack of detergent and the premium shampoo, and left him the recharge, the loose commodity and the emergency purchase at nine at night.

His response has been to carry less inventory and turn it faster. A carton that sits for a month is money he could have used elsewhere, and he has learned that the salesman will come again, or that the wholesaler's number is in his phone. What used to be a monthly relationship has become a weekly transaction.
"Earlier I filled the shelf and waited for the month; now I fill what will move by Sunday," said a kirana owner in the market lane, tallying the day's credit entries in a notebook.
The dark store at four in the morning

The dark store near the college area runs on a schedule the rest of the trade never sees. A replenishment vehicle arrives before dawn, and by six the pickers have restocked the racks against the previous day's demand pattern. Its assortment is narrow by kirana standards, a few thousand items chosen on velocity, and it holds almost nothing that does not move.

That is the structural difference, and everyone in the chain understands it. The kirana carries range for a neighbourhood and finances it himself. The dark store carries velocity for an algorithm and finances it centrally. The distributor sits between the two, holding range on behalf of a company and being paid on velocity.
Redrawing the plan again

The distributor's own plan for the year is not dramatic. He is adding two smaller towns on the highway where no platform operates and where the wholesaler's reach is weaker. He is putting one salesman on a route dedicated to the larger outlets, and moving the smallest shops to a fortnightly cycle with a telephone order in between.

He is also, for the first time, asking one of his principals for a coverage-linked payment rather than a pure turnover margin. He expects to be refused this year and to be heard next year. The beat plan on his desk has three sets of corrections on it, in three different pens.
